title_x: The value of this laptop comes from detail
text:
This ABC 17 is a system for a well-informed professional without much budget constraints. Such a person would value presentation, portability and pixel count over raw performance, but they also have enough computing needs to refuse to compromise too much on performance.
Value: If you just want to game on a laptop, you can get basically the same GPU of RTX 2060 and a better AMD cpu of Ryzen 4900hs from the ASUS Zephyrus G14. At $1400 as of this review, the Zephryrus is a far more attractive option based on the numbers. However, there are many details FusionTech put onto this laptop that makes it possibly worth the +$1000 premium (As of this review, the current generation ABC 17 can be as low as $2400 depending on where you look)
Screen: If you have good eyes and a need for screen pixel estate, the glossy 4K+ screen is absolutely gorgeous and can fit a ton of windows and spreadsheets when scaled to 100%. The touchscreen adds a way to efficiently interact with it. This screen is basically bezel-less, you get 17” of screen in a laptop the size of a 15” laptop, indeed I was able to fit this laptop in a bag compartment for 15” laptops only where my old 17” gaming laptop would definitely not fit. The high resolution and normal (I assume 60hz) refresh rate makes it a productivity machine, as opposed to gaming machines with lower resolution and higher refresh rates.
GPU: You can game with modern titles, but games would not necessarily be able to run at 4K and still get a good framerate. Compared to my 4 year old gaming laptop with an nVidia GTX 980M, the RTX 2060 max-q in the ABC offers basically the same performance and some new features in a much smaller package. And I know my GTX 980M struggled with games a lot, even at 1080p. The 2060 Max Q is considered “VR-ready” and most games developed for VR should be playable, however normal games with VR mode are more demanding and could struggle to run.
CPU: The only reason to choose Intel for this generation is if there are some Intel-specific features you need for your work, or if the rest of the laptop happens to be quite good as is the case here and you’re willing to compromise on the CPU. While by no means a slouch, you are not getting the best laptop CPU in terms of performance and efficiency. The Intel I9-10885H is worse than the AMD R9 4900HS in every way with higher power consumption and lower processing speed, the only exception being slightly better single thread performance - a small consolation in a world where developers are used to optimizing apps for multiple threads. A workload I use a lot is x264 video encoding. Measuring the power draw and frames processed over 12 hours, the i9 has double the efficiency as my 5 year old i7, but 20% less efficiency than my desktop ryzen 3900x. Less efficiency also means more heat: with ideal cooling conditions (a 50W box fan blowing on the laptop), the CPU was able to draw about 90W more power than idle.
As a system, the CPU+GPU combination was able to playback youtube 8K60 content with no stuttering.
Ports: I like the ports on this laptop, there are 4 thunderbolt/type C ports which serve to both transmit data and charge the laptop. A 130W usb C charger is included, you can also charge using a USB PD (Power Delivery) charger. This is exciting as it opens up the possibility of charging a full size gaming laptop from a USB C power bank via the PD protocol: My current on-the-go tablet, a Surface 3, was purchased entirely on the basis that at the time, it was the fastest windows powered x86 machine I could get that could be charged from a power bank.
Battery: A fully charged battery can last more than 3 hours of casual use, or 90 minutes with the CPU at 100%. My attempts to charge the ABC 17 from various power banks 10W-60W and prolong its runtime when not connected to mains, were met with limited success: Starting with both batteries at 100% hoping that the power bank would slow down the discharge rate, older power banks simply would not charge. Newer power banks would connect, but because type c to type c is non directional, the laptop would attempt to charge the power bank instead of letting the power bank charge it (there doesn’t seem to be a software switch to toggle direction of power). Finally, the PD power banks appeared to start charging the laptop after the laptop’s battery dropped below 80%.
Dongle: The laptop has only type C ports so regular peripherals will need to be connected via dongles or hubs. A basic HDMI+USBA dongle is included in the package. There are many dongles but I recommend getting one with full 4K 60hz video output and 100W PD, which allows you to charge the laptop through the dongle while freeing up the other ports for more dongles! A well-made single dongle will simultaneously: transfer 4K60 video signal to an external screen, copy files from external usb A hard disks and internal sd card readers at combined 200 megabytes/s, pipe in 900 megabits/s of internet upload/download, and power the laptop from an external PD power source
Longevity: This laptop includes the “FusionTech Power Manager” utility that allows you to limit charge to a number less than 100% if you keep your laptop plugged in all the time. Keeping batteries topped off at 100% is bad for longevity – I’ve experienced multiple battery failures on devices I need to leave plugged in 24/7. Capping charge at 60% will maximize battery longevity while 80% will give you a bit more flexibility if there is a power outage or if you need your laptop for an unplanned excursion. If you don’t know what percentage to use, you can leave Power Manager on auto or set it to one of several presets. The technology to limit charging has been around for ages, disappointingly not all manufacturers include this function. The ABC is also a model where you don’t have to worry about availability and instructions for replacing the battery.
Software: Windows Hello, using infrared facial recognition to unlock the PC, is a very convenient alternative to passwords. 365 days of McAfee LiveSafe are included although I have not had good experiences with McAfee antivirus in the past.
Keyboard: In exchange for the lack of a numpad, you get normal sized backlit keys and nice speakers on the sides of the keyboard. The way the Fn key works is interesting as an inversion of how Fn usually works: the F1/ F2… keys activate the Fn functions by default, if you want to input F4 you have to press Fn+F4. Commands like Alt+F4 still work as usual.
Condition: The specs and condition of my unit appeared to be as described and there was no malfunction or inaccuracy in any way.
Summary: If you know what you’re getting into, the current generation FusionTech ABC 17 is a quality asset to your professional or personal needs, engineered for the long haul. A pricey machine that maximizes the utility of a portable small size, the ABC 17 is capable of gaming but best used for productivity or entertainment where fine detail makes a difference.

title_x: Amazing workstation power in a travel size. Excellent for science/video/engineering, decent gaming
text:
For years, manufacturers have offered three types of laptops:

Low powered productivity centers (good for surfing, watching a movie, writing)
High powered "gaming" laptops (good graphics/cpu/memory, but terrible battery life and chunky/heavy)
Sleek high end business laptops (better memory, better battery, better processor, but mediocre graphics)

More recently, a fourth class has arrived. These are laptops that offer most of what gaming laptops have, but are sleeker, lighter, and with far better battery. These tend to be expensive. But they offer a portable experience you can't otherwise get.

This is one of these modern laptops. While, at 5 pounds, 7 ounces, no one is going to call this svelt (I reserve that term for my ~2lb Surface tablet+keyboard), it's very thin, offers a 17" 4K screen, high end Quadro graphics, a lot of memory, and a fast enough processor.

Honestly, as a computational scientist who uses computers to do intensive calculations on CPUs and GPUs for molecular design, this is the laptop I've been waiting for. The performance of this laptop is pretty close to that of the large HP Z440 tower that I use at home for the same sorts of things.

Since the Amazon listing is fairly incomplete, let me fill in the details of this laptop:

Screen: 17" WQUXGA (3840x2400) touchscreen @60Hz
Processor: Intel I7 10750H / 2.6Ghz (6 cores, 12 threads)
Memory: 32Gb RAM (2 slots, 16Gb each, user replaceable)
Disk: 512Gb NVMe
Graphics: Nvidia Quadro RTX-3000 Max-Q
Webcam: 720p with Windows "Hello" support
Fingerprint scanner integrated into power on button.
Windows Pro 10 x64 installed
Chipset: Intel Mobile WM-490
WiFi: Intel WiFi 6 (AX-201)
Card Reader: SD/SDHC/SDXC
Included charger: 130W, USB-C interface
Interface ports: 4 x USB-C Gen 2 / Thunderbolt 3 ports. All support power delivery; 1 x audio minijack
Battery: 6-cell 97W battery

While there are faster processors available (high end Ryzen and Intel I9), unless you're running an app that pegs the processor in multi-thread (parallel) mode, you won't notice that difference. 32Gb is the sweet spot in terms of memory for a high end laptop. And they've chose to go with the Max-Q variant of the Quadro GPU, which trades off a bit of performance (underclocking) for better power and heat management. Again, if you are running an app that takes full advantage of every spec of GPU performance, you might notice this. But the average person won't, day to day. And it buys you a LOT in terms of battery life and portability.

Although I'm not much of a gamer myself, I ran two respected benchmarks to evaluate this laptop as a gaming machine: 3DMark and Novabench. Predictably, both peg this is a solid mid-line gaming laptop. (See photos). You can buy a laptop that does better at games. But most of those run only 1-3 hours in full gaming mode, tend to be heavy, and are very expensive. If you are the kind of person who needs the absolute bleeding edge in gaming (and you know if you are), then this isn't the laptop for you. But if you're a scientist or business person who occasionally likes to play games, this laptop will HANDILY perform for you (and offer the benefit of better design and battery life).

Under stress this laptop moves a LOT of air through the ports on the bottom (and out through the back of the laptop). You will definitely notice the whir of the fans. That said, unless you're stressing the cpu or gpu, the fans are quite quiet. The keyboard got warm under stress, but not uncomfortable. At top speed, the fans generate roughly 45dB of noise. I did not observe any obvious thermal throttling, even under stress loads.

I would rate the feel of the keyboard a "B". It gets the job done, but I would have liked a bit more travel for the keys. The touchpad is responsive and works fine, but there, I would have preferred separate mouse buttons. I am not a fan of mouse buttons integrated into the bottom of the touchpad, such as we have here. The touchpad is giant--a plus. The keyboard is backlit (adjustable). That's also a plus.

The camera is one of the big letdowns here. The integrated webcam supports only 720p (1280x720). Given that this is indisputably a high end laptop, I am surprised they didn't go with a higher resolution webcam. That said, the sensor seems pretty good, and the picture is acceptably bright (see photo). It gets the job done, but hopefully next they up the optics.

In terms of ports, you get 4x USB-C (Gen 3, rev 2, i.e. 10Mbps) that can also function as Thunderbolt ports, plus a SD card reader. That's it. Two USB-C ports are on each side of the laptop. There are no ports in the front or back. While the number of Thunderbolt-enabled peripherals is still low (and the number that aren't outrageously priced is lower still), Thunderbolt offers FAR greater speeds: 40 Mbps vs 10 Mbps for USB-C (Gen rev 2) (and vs 5Mbps for good old USB-A 3.0). The Thunderbolt 3 standard also provides for power delivery of up to 100W, up to 10Gb networking, and is fast enough to support a high end external video card. Bottom line is this: The future for Thunderbolt looks great, and with this laptop you are probably future-proofed on that front for several years.

While I love that this laptop supports Thunderbolt 3 (and all four ports are Thunderbolt 3), it is annoying that FusionTech didn't bother to include at least one USB-A port. A lot of recent peripherals (e.g. mice and keyboards) still have a USB-A cable. I know I can go with Bluetooth enabled devices, but that's not always the best plan. Oh well. FusionTech does include a dongle that you plug into one of the USB-C ports and it provides both a USB-A and HDMI connection. Just know that whatever you attach to this laptop, outside of USB-C/ Thunderbolt devices, is going to require an adapter.

In terms of security, it was nice to find that this laptop supports Windows "Hello" face recognition, which, in addition to the standard Webcam, requires IR cameras. You can see the IR camera working when you log in--you'll see blinking red lights next to the Webcam (see photos).

WiFi is provided by Intel's latest and greatest mobile chip, the AX-201. This supports the latest standard, WiFi 6, along with providing backward compatibility to all previous WiFi standards. It's an excellent performer. Bluetooth 5.1 support goes along with the AX-201.

The stereo speakers sound very good for laptop speakers. There are two top-focused speakers and two bottom-focused speakers, with a total of 5W. The sound is clean and (by laptop standards) loud. These are among the best-sounding laptop speakers I've ever encountered.

The screen is very bright (531 nits) and very clear, with great contrast (1590:1). It has a anti-glare flat finish (rather than matte), which is my preference. It's also a touchscreen, which is nice. The screen bends back but does not flip over (i.e. you can't use this as a glorified tablet). The screen quality is actually unusually good for a laptop and is suitable for work where a good color gamut is required. The bezel around the screen is extremely thin, allow the 17" screen to be fitted within as small a package as possible.

Given the specs and abilities of this laptop (including the 17" 4K screen), battery life is nothing short of outstanding: I got slightly under 10 hours of surfing/productivity app use on a full battery. Unlike most gaming laptops, this laptop will easily last the entirety of most airplane trips.

Two aspects of the laptop can be user-upgraded: The memory and the storage. The laptop has two memory slots, which are both occupied (with 16Gb each, or 32Gb total). The chipset used in this laptop can support up to 128Gb of memory. There are also two NVMe slots, one of which carries the 512Gb storage that comes with this laptop. The memory that came with the laptop I got is SK Hynix PC 611. This is a middle-of-the-road NVMe SSD. FusionTech does have a tendency to change vendors for the storage, so you may get something different.

To replace/upgrade the memory or storage, you will need to remove the bottom of the laptop. This requires removing eight screws from the bottom panel using a T5 Torx driver and a prying tool to get the bottom panel to snap off the body. It's not incredibly hard, but it could be made easier. In particular, the need to carefully pry the bottom off is annoying. (I have included a picture showing the inside once you remove the cover, pointing out where the replaceable components (memory, SSD, battery) are located. )

But that's a minor nit.

Honestly, there is a lot to love about this laptop, and very little to complain about. It really hits the sweet spot of combining tremendous workstation-level performance, a good video card, quality construction, a great screen, excellent speakers, and excellent battery life. It's not cheap, but the best things in life seldom are.

If you need workstation level performance--if you use your laptop for CAD, AI, videography, science, or any other field where you need high-end cpu/graphics/video performance and a high resolution, high quality display, this is the laptop you should be looking at.

text:
[[VIDEOID:23785d7ed3d89d14d8e3c26fb04f5801]] The Advance M15 R4 measures 10.86” x 14.19” x 0.78” and weighs 5 and a half pounds. The M15 R4 comes with a 15.6” 1080p display with 300 nits of brightness and 100%sRGD color gamut. My device was configured with the Intel Core i7-10870H, an RTX 3070 8GB GDDR6, 16GB of 2933MHz DDR4 RAM, a 1-TB SSD, and Killer Wi-Fi 6 AX1650i 802.11ax 2x2 Wireless LAN + Bluetooth 5.1.

I use this laptop daily for everything from coding and web development to gaming and everything in-between. When companies speak of desktop replacement laptops the Advance M15 R4 is precisely what they mean as you can get all the performance and power of a desktop in the footprint of a laptop.

What I liked most about the Advance M15 R4 was:
- Typing Experience. Other than the screen size, the thing I miss most when transitioning from a desktop to a laptop is keyboard. With a desktop I usually take advantage of a mechanical keyboard. At times, (like now) I switch things up and use a chicklet-style keyboard, but I prefer mechanical keyboards. This Advance computer comes with a mechanical keyboard that splits the difference between a chicklet keyboard and a mechanical one. The Advance’s keyboard gives the satisfying feedback of a mechanical keyboard while minimizing the sound. You don’t get the full travel distance of a standard desktop keyboard but the amount of key travel you get on the Advance is exceptional in relation to most other laptops.

- Display. I work online in IT and am a web development student at night. Color accuracy is very important for me, and I have been quite impressed by the vibrancy of this display. Colors are vivid and the screen is bright. Scrolling to test the webpages I create is a joy because I know that any hiccups, I encounter are most likely a result of bad code instead of a display that cannot keep up with how swiftly I am navigating a page. For gaming, the same holds true. Images are sharp and bright. Combining this display with a 3070 allows for insane framerates on some titles.

- Performance. I own two desktop computers that were both in heavy use before the Advance arrived. One is a FusionTech OptiPlex sleeper system that’s rocking an i-5 2400 and a GTX 1650 Super. The other is an M1 Mac Mini. The OptiPlex is good for most gaming titles I play. The M1 Mac Mini is a beast in its own right, particularly for productivity and creative tasks. Still, neither of those computers offer the versatility and performance of the Advance. While there are Mac OS exclusive titles I use for creating content that keep the M1 Mac Mini in heavy rotation for my workflow, the Advance M15 R4 has made my OptiPlex obsolete. I’ve uploaded images of my current desktop setup which includes the Advance and the M1 Mac Mini with both attached to a 34” 1440p display.

- Aesthetics. I remember falling in love with the Big Bang Theory television show a several years ago and my favorite character, Sheldon Cooper, was often found perched behind an Advance PC. That distinctive glowing head has evolved over time into something that is much more elegant and refined. The Tron lights on the back, UFO aircraft vents on the underbelly and below the display, and the customizable lights all embrace the legacy design language of Advance computers while updating it for modern times. When I meet up with other development students at our favorite Coffeeshop I see several MacBook computers. I’m the only one who has an Advance and while I initially received looks of condescension it didn’t take long for critics to become enamored with the Advance aesthetic. Very often now I hear, “You know, Apple should do a bit more with its logo, don’t you think?”

- Gaming. I saved gaming for last because gaming is last in my life right now if I am being completely honest. Between work, school, and commitments with the girlfriend my gaming time is usually around an hour a month. That said, when I do game, I can run practically anything thanks to Advance opting for the more power-hungry variant of the mobile RTX 3070 than the 30% less powerful version that was once named Max Q. I ran several benchmarks of this computer; however, Amazon only allows for one video upload per review. The video benchmark I uploaded was run on 3DMark as it’s been trusted for years. This system scored over 10000 on the Time Spy benchmark. The CPU temperature maxed at 95 C and while the GPU max temperature rose to 68 C.

A couple of disclaimers on these benchmarks. First, I captured the benchmark on my phone vs OBS or any other screen capture program but there’s still room for performance improvement. If you look in the lower right corner of the video, you’ll notice several notifications are present which indicate running programs. There’s even a Windows update icon showing in the notification center. I intentionally ran this benchmark on an unoptimized system because I think many gamers are like me in that they work, go to school, and/or generally have other things to do rather than optimize their system to get the absolute best performance before each time they game. For those reasons I think it’s possible to improve performance.

What I liked least about the Advance M15 R4 was:
- Warranty Experience. Immediately after I setup my Advance PC I registered it and started receiving notifications about extending the warranty. FusionTech makes this process as close to the 1980’s used car buying experience as possible by not making it possible to purchase an extended warranty online. Instead, you have to talk to some greedy salesperson working in a foreign country who will force you to haggle your way into the best price over a series of calls and supposed ‘meetings with a manager.’ Inevitably, I was told a single year of extended warranty coverage at the base level would cost $349 with the best coverage costing $449 for a single year. A 2-year warranty would cost as much as $899. Needless to say, I declined to pay that price but am stuck having private number calls bombarding my cellphone with requests for me to continue haggling for better pricing. FusionTech should just make the best price available online and let customers sign up that way. The only purpose this call-in requirement has is to force customers to give in and pay more than they should to protect their devices due to high-pressure sales.

- Thermals. One of the compromises to expect with a high-powered laptop that’s stuffed into a small footprint is high thermals. The keyboard warms a bit when this system is cranking out 100+ frames in a competitive game. Consequently, the fans crank up which generates a substantial amount of fan noise. Neither of these issues bother me but I wanted to disclose this for others.

- Battery life. Depending on how much a person taxes this machine its battery can last as long as 4 hours or as short as an hour and a half. Personally, I keep my device plugged in most of the time as I use this Advance M15 R4 as a desktop replacement 95% of the time. However, when I do take it to the coffeeshop to show it off I find battery life is quite poor, particularly in comparison to M1 MacBook Air computers.

Overall, this Advance M15 R4 is the perfect desktop replacement computer. The Advance is an aesthetically pleasing piece of high-performing technology that boasts a bright, color-accurate display, and exceptional performance as both a gaming and development PC. I absolutely loathed every aspect of attempting to extend the warranty and had to mention the impact thermals and battery life have on the user experience. 4.5 out of 5.0

text:
First, please be aware that Amazon often mixes reviews for various optional models on a single item’s page. That is the case with the reviews here.

THIS review is specifically for the FusionTech ABC 9700 17-inch Ultra High-Definition+ Touch Screen laptop with the 1Tb NVMe hard drive, the 6-cell (97 Watt-Hour) battery, the 130-Watt rapid charger, 10th Generation Intel Core i9-10885H processor, 32 Gb RAM, Qualcomm Killer AX500s DBS Wi-Fi module, Bluetooth 5.2, and the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 video graphics processor with 6Gb dedicated memory to supplement the built-in Intel UHD Graphics 630 CPU based graphics.

This is, by all measures, a top-of-the-line powerful, capable, and stylish laptop with excellent battery life, fast charging, and an amazingly sharp and bright display. Despite its slim and sleek profile, it is a workhorse with an amazingly large 17” screen in a package just a half inch deeper than my old HP 15.4-inch laptop and much thinner and lighter. Open, it has a handsome “carbon fiber” look keyboard platform, a huge touch-pad, and that stunning wide-viewing-angle 3840 X 2400 9.2 Megapixel screen with a minuscule .0954mm pixel pitch. Closed, it is all metal on the outside.

As I began to put it through its various usability tests, I found that the laptop was, as expected, amazingly fast and responsive. Cold boot times are on the order of 20-25 seconds from opening the lid (if using facial recognition sign on) and wake-up from sleep averages 7-9 seconds.

I configure the laptop to use three different sign-on schemes, PIN, fingerprint reader, and facial recognition. As expected, PIN works flawlessly every time but if it is a number only PIN, the lack of a dedicated number pad on the keyboard slows entry somewhat. FusionTech could perhaps have chosen to narrow the keys and relocate the two stereo speakers that flank the keyboard thereby gaining enough space for a number pad, but it would have required that the keyboard be compact instead of the comfortably large standard-size keys that are a joy to type on.

After configuring the fingerprint reader, it too flawlessly recognized my fingerprint quickly and reliably every time and rejected all other attempts at using the wrong fingerprint. It is, in this application a viable security method in my opinion. Lastly, I engaged the facial recognition feature of sign-in. This means that you will need to allow camera operation, so the typical piece of tape over the camera practiced by paranoid users will defeat this function. It is, by far, the fastest and easiest of the sign-in options and, like the fingerprint reader, accurate and reliable. I did a little testing whether it could be fooled by a good picture or a selfie on a large tablet, and it did not respond to those “hacks”, but like any security system, I’m sure it can be defeated with enough effort. Still, it worked perfectly for me scores of times using my actual face.

Once all the Windows set-up questions were completed, I began installing various programs and applications for my use. Since, like most modern “slim” laptops, this computer lacks a CD / DVD drive, I had to employ an external one to load some of my older applications. The laptop comes with a pair of USB 3.2 Gen 2, DisplayPort 1.4 (supporting up to HBR2), Thunderbolt 3 ports on each side, and using a USB C to USB A adapter, my old external drive was immediately recognized.

The ABC 17 came with some FusionTech applications pre-installed. Some may consider them as “bloat-ware,” although I found many of them useful. FusionTech’s Support Assistant, for instance, keeps drivers up to date and performs a “tune-up” on demand. Similarly, FusionTech Power Manager is very useful for customizing battery life. I recommend giving them a chance and deciding which ones are useful for you and removing the rest later.

During extensive use testing, I ran up against some limitations of the included Windows 10 Home operating system. Therefore, after a few weeks, I upgraded the OS to Windows 10 Pro using a complete reformat and clean install. This required that I re-visit the FusionTech support site and re-install some of the more useful FusionTech utilities and features, but I found the process to be smooth and trouble free. Once win 10 Pro was installed, I began to work the computer in earnest.

If you use very processor-intensive applications the two internal fans will spool up and can be somewhat noisy, but during typical use they rarely engage. During high resolution gaming, expect the fans to run continuously at varying speeds. Temperature control seems adequate to keep the outside of the laptop comfortably cool. For a slim laptop, the built-in speakers and two rear “subwoofer” ports provide remarkably good sound. The built-in sound card can drive a full multi-channel setup given the right external adapter and speakers.

The lack of a LAN port (RJ-45) was almost always compensated by the very capable and strong Wi-Fi adapter that connected almost instantly to either of my two home wireless networks whenever the computer was awakened. But, in the interest of running some file transfer tests across my LAN, to and from my NAS servers, I acquired an Anker 11-in-1 USB 3 hub that allows for a wired Ethernet connection (among many other options).

Using the Anker hub, and running many hours of tests, I discovered that the laptop’s built-in USB 3.2 ports can handle virtually any challenge at top speed. Not once did the laptop limit transfer speeds. Rather, the limits of the Gigabit LAN or the hardware of the various external drives I used determined maximum speeds. Additionally, the hub allowed me to use two external 1080p monitors, and although the ports are rated up to 4K, unfortunately I did not have any displays to test that with. The laptop easily supports external displays in “duplicate” or “extended desktop” modes.

Next, I ran the laptop on battery power alone during a routine day of authoring and browsing and emailing via the Wi-Fi connection. Battery life was exceptional despite purposely running the display at higher than recommended brightness. After nearly 7 hours of work with few interruptions the battery meter still read around 18%. Using the supplied 130-Watt charger, it recovered the full charge in just under two hours, which makes this one of the most portable and usable field machines I have ever used. My vehicle, which has a 110V outlet in the console and a built-in Wi-Fi hotspot make for an exceptionally productive mobile office using this computer.

When you first get started with this high-end laptop, you will undoubtedly find that some of the functions do not perform exactly the way you want them to. One of the most important is how the touch-pad responds to your touch. I need to say, unequivocally, that THIS laptop is NOT the one so many reviewers have panned for its touch-pad issues. First, there are many settings that can be applied to customize the touch-pad sensitivity, response, and functions. This touch-pad is glorious to use. It is big enough to allow for incredible pointing detail and can easily be set to move the cursor fully across the screen with a single swipe. It makes “Click and Drag” functions fast and simple. The touch-pad is rock solid, doesn’t move in its frame, is silent, and bulls-eye accurate. All the multiple finger gestures are supported and customizable. It works so well that I hardly, if ever, resort to the touch screen. There is, of course, an option to add an external mouse, and even a setting that allows you to have the built-in touch pad turn off when you connect the mouse so you can use the panel as a wrist rest without inadvertently moving the cursor.

If, while you are using this laptop, you find one of its functions annoying or imperfect, it’s my belief that buried somewhere in Windows or a FusionTech app, there’s a setting for it that will allow you to fine tune it to your liking. You just may have to hunt for it.

This is an ideal, fast, beautiful business / graphics laptop that will work at lightning speed to get your jobs done. It’s a high-rez, clear-screen gamer with a very fast and capable NVIDIA graphics adapter. It’s a looker, and easy to carry, charge, and use. Information storage and retrieval is virtually instant due to the fast i9 CPU and the extremely fast and huge NVMe drive. It is fast booting and runs most apps at blazing speeds.

But, I do have a few quibbles to comment on perhaps to prove that nothing is perfect.

First, for me, it’s a shame that such a powerful laptop comes with Win 10 Home, not Win 10 Pro. Since it is such a strong business machine, I would expect that it will be used in a domain environment. Win 10 Home does not support domains, nor do they allow remote access. You have to upgrade to Pro for $99 retail to fix that.

Next, there is an included USB 3 adapter to hook an external display and any standard USB-A cabled accessory, but it does not have a LAN port. Again, in business , you may want to hook to a wired network for internal security, and that requires a third party adapter. Both adapters I did try to use for this worked flawlessly and at full LAN speeds though.

The camera is weak. It only supports 1280 by 720 resolution, which given the exceptional graphics screen on this machine, is inadequate. It does work just fine for conferencing though.

Ergonomically, three things strike me as negatives. One, the case is actually hard to open, as it has no real grip point on the front to swing open the screen and it is stiff to open. Maybe it will loosen with time. Second, you cannot fold this back to use it as a tablet, despite the touch screen. To me, that is truly minor, but others may feel it is more important. Third, the front edge of the body where one naturally rests one’s hand when using the touch-pad is not rounded in any way. It is a sharply defined edge that eventually irritates the heel of your hand after hours of use. I started using an external mouse when I intended to work long hours on it.

Lastly, the computer comes with some “bloat-ware.” Some is from Microsoft, some is from FusionTech. Some of the included apps are actually useful, but I found some to be just a waste of storage space. Your needs may dictate that you will have to systematically remove some of these apps.

In conclusion, this is a fabulous high-end laptop. Comparing it to my brother’s premium Macbook Pro, it is very similar in performance and yet is considerably less expensive than the Mac. It is backed by what I consider to be an industry leader in support and service and backed by a very extensive support website. It never crashed, faltered, or failed to run anything I tasked it with. It has industry leading battery life and recharge times, and is satisfyingly fast.

As well as it performed, there is no way that my few negative points could add up to detract even a half a star from my unequivocal 5-star rating. If you need a monster laptop in a demure package with an all-day battery, this is your machine.

title_x: An Overall Excellent Computer With A Few Issues
text:
[[VIDEOID:b5e29231068f7a642779e2bb9bd7162f]] TL;DR - This is a very powerful laptop - if that’s what you’re looking for, it will not disappoint. It games well, looks good and can double as a space heater when under load! I think the price is justified based on what it includes spec-wise and the mostly-premium build quality. But I have a lot more to say, so read on if you’re interested.

Yes, I got this for free through Vine. No, that will not influence my review - if anything it makes me more stringent because I have nothing to lose. I’m a Mac guy and have been since the switch to Intel in 2006. I prefer macOS over Windows any and every day of the week. But, as we all know there’s quite the Apple tax on their hardware. My current Mac is a 2018 Mini that does alright, but lacks the oomph of modern machines in some tasks. While browsing the Vine items one day I saw this laptop and once I realized what it was, I ordered it immediately. I mean, who doesn’t want a free Advance computer!? I was pretty excited to get it. I’m also NOT an avid gamer - Nintendo classics are my jam and it’s rare that I spend much time playing a game start to finish. But I am a hobbyist photographer so I can and do appreciate the value of a powerful computer and am looking forward to using it for editing my photos. So although this m15 will not see as much game time as most will, I still feel pretty confident I can give it a fair review. So here goes…

First off - if you don’t need the powerhouse that is this laptop, DO NOT BUY IT! There are other similarly spec’d machines that are far more practical than this. This is more like a gaming computer first, and a laptop second. It’s big, kinda heavy, runs really hot, burns through the battery quickly (even when not gaming) and overall is just a lot of computer. It can only use the dedicated GPU, not the one integrated into the CPU because of the 300Hz screen, so there are just no power savings to be had. The fans are always on, though the speed varies of course, and using it in your lap gets it hot quick. Using it on a flat surface where all the vents are usable is the best bet. Once you unplug it, the battery drains quickly. I used it for about 2 hours for just web browsing type stuff and I was approaching dead by the time I finished. I played a game (Forza Horizon 4) on battery for 20-ish minutes and I was at 40% battery remaining. So true portability is not what this computer’s about - sure it’s portable in the sense that it can be picked up and brought somewhere, but you’ll never want to be too far from a power source. Another note about the fans - they are loud when gaming. They’re not quite as high-pitched and annoying as your usual laptop fans, but if you want to hear your game you better have headphones or a loud-enough sound system to overpower the fan noise. The internal speakers get plenty loud, but when you’re sitting right in front of the machine it’s tough to not hear the fans. The touchpad is pretty small for 2021, but it’s definitely usable and very responsive. It also stinks that the RAM is soldered and not upgradeable after purchase - this is a trend in the industry, although not a good one in my opinion. I know a touch screen is not necessary for a gaming laptop, but seems like it should be a “throw in” for what this costs. I also wish the card reader was full-size SD instead of micro, but that’s nothing a USB one can’t fix. But the silver lining to all of that - everything you do with this machine is FAST! I didn’t do a deep dive into performance settings, but whatever throttling algorithms are in place do well enough to make the experience a pleasant one - no matter what the task.

How about the things I do love? The overall design is great. It has a premium look and feel to it. There’s a nice combination of plastic and aluminum, the latter of which seems to be coated with something. With the RGB lights off it doesn’t scream “gaming laptop” with the exception of the alien on the back. And speaking of the RGB lights, those are really cool too and the fact you can customize them is great. I wish the screen was 4K, but 1080p is fine for my 37-year-old eyes - everything looks plenty sharp. It seems to be pretty color accurate and the brightness is good too. The keyboard is a little “clicky” for long-winded typing sessions, but it’s very nice to type on aside from that. The speakers are pretty great as far as laptop speakers go, so no real complaints there. It’s also awesome that there is space for THREE SSDs inside. Being out of the gaming scene for a while, I had no idea how large game downloads have gotten - but now I understand why someone might need all three! Regardless, it’s still awesome. I was able to use Lightroom and Photoshop (to edit the photos for this review, nonetheless) with ease. Everything was fluid and responsive. I imagine a machine spec’d like this one would do great with video editing as well.

I don’t have access to any of the usual suspects as far as benchmarking goes, so instead I used the Benchmark Mode of Forza Horizon 4. Using the laptop screen’s resolution of 1920x1080 with the FPS cranked up to 300, it averaged about 134. Since the human eyes can’t really see that many FPS, I turned it back down to a more-reasonable 75 FPS and it had no problem maintaining that. I then connected it to my 4K Samsung TV via HDMI - at the TV’s native resolution of 3840x2160 it breezed through the test again at 60 FPS, which is the highest my TV can support - I think. You can see screenshots of the results attached to my review. Worth noting is that when I had the TV connected and both displays active, I had tons of stuttering and low frame rates even when only showing the game on one of them. I’m not sure if this is the GPU showing its limitations or me not setting something up correctly.

So as nice as this machine is, there are a few things that have left me unimpressed - especially when the cost for this is almost $2,200 at the time of review. The screen has a lot of backlight bleed on dark screens (see photo) - this just should not happen at this price point. And the screen is pretty flexible - not in a good way. You can see it visibly flexing if you only use one hand to open the lid. Not to the point of breakage of course, but I would expect some more rigidity. And mine seems to be permanently bent slightly - there’s an ever-so-small gap on the left side between the screen and the palm rest when the lid is closed. Also, at least on my particular machine, the RGB lights under the keys have a bit of a gremlin. When I have the lights turned off I still see some green flashes under the right-hand area from time to time. And, as shown in my video, it seems to react to taps on the bezel. This does not appear to be an intended feature but rather a malfunction. Luckily it doesn’t affect anything else, but I imagine it will get worse over time. When I took my computer out of the box for the first time, I could see some scuffs near the power port - looks like it was some careless employee in the testing part of assembly. Lastly, and this could just be a Microsoft thing, but it locked up during the initial setup of Windows - I had to shut it down forcefully and reboot.

All that said, this is a great computer. I anticipate using it for many years to come. It’s flaws are negligible in comparison to the whole package. Had I truly spent $2,200 on it it there’s no way I wouldn’t exchange it to get rid of the RGB gremlins and to try for a display with less backlight bleed (it varies from panel to panel). But if you get a perfect one, I truly believe you’ve gotten your money’s worth. Just make sure you put everything through its paces before the end of your return period.

text:
I have had this FusionTech ABC 9500 for six months and it's a disaster.

This is my third or fourth FusionTech laptop and both this one and its predecessor (a FusionTech Sharp) have BIG problems. The biggest problem is that the battery swells. As you can see in the photos, as the battery swells, the touch pad starts to lift up and you can no longer click on it. Eventually the whole front of the case separates so you can no longer properly close the computer. More importantly, this is extremely dangerous because if the pouch of a lithium ion battery ruptures it will likely result in an explosion. This is totally unacceptable and never happened in the other brands of laptops I used over the years.

Second, with the FusionTech ABC 9500 I have had frequent problems with the screen going mostly black, and I have to push down on the screen or wiggle it to get the screen to come back up. A FusionTech service person said they fixed it by updating my drivers but the nature of the problem (and the fact that wiggling the monitor makes it come back to life) makes me think this probably isn't a driver problem. Only time will tell (I just had the drivers updated a few days ago).

Third, the headphone jack doesn't work. It only had hissing and static, and then I had an in-home FusionTech service call and they replaced the bottom of the computer and now there is no sound from the headphone jack at all. On top of that, the person lost three of the screws from the bottom of the computer and only screwed in one of the other five about halfway.

Last but not least, this computer was chosen for me by my employer and when it arrived I discovered it only had USB-C ports -- no regular USB ports. Since all of my peripherals are USB (microphone, mouse, tablet, ring light, MIDI keyboard), I have to use an adapter dongle for absolutely everything, and the dongle won't power the MIDI keyboard. It's beyond frustrating.

All in all, this computer has been way too much trouble and I'm going to try to have my employer return it and I will avoid FusionTechs until there is some evidence they have solved their quality control problems.

title_x: Maybe the most frustrating PC I have ever had.
text: This computer is great for the most part. That said, I have had several issues since purchasing it. When I first received the computer, I had issues with it not wanting to run certain games that I had on Steam. Several games would not start. Instead, I received a popup regarding missing .dll files. I didn't blame this on the computer though. About three months after purchasing this computer, it overheated and fried the hard drive out of NOWHERE. The computer was asleep and closed. The following morning, I went to use it and it was hot to the touch. I opened the computer and shut it down (from the login screen). I let the computer cool off for a while. When I came back to it and turned it on, the computer sent me to a startup error screen. I sent the computer to FusionTech for warranty repairs, and it came back better than ever. Or so I thought. One day, I went to play a game and was notified that my drivers were pretty old. This confused me, so I went to open the GeForce Experience application. Huh. My computer does not detect that I have a GeForce GTX graphics card. I still have this issue today - whenever it occurs, I just have to restart my PC. It's annoying, but I figured it probably wasn't my computer. A few months later, I went to my mother's house. We decided to watch a movie, but she did not have a smart TV. When we plugged the HDMI cable into my computer, nothing happened. I thought it was the cable, but we plugged the same cable into another laptop and everything worked perfectly. I am now having issues with my USB ports. All three USB ports will provide power to a device, but that is it. This becomes an issue when you need to use an external mouse. No matter what I do, I cannot get any external mice to work. I use this computer for school and gaming. While I can do all of my school work with a trackpad, gaming is another story. This computer seriously runs great, but there have been so many hardware issues that I felt like I needed to write this review. Perhaps I just got a dud? Who knows? I do have Avast Premium antivirus, and I use a VPN every time I connect to the internet. I am kind of a computer nerd, and I care a lot about my computer's security, so I am not like your grandmother who clicks on everything she sees. That said, I don't believe my issues are caused by malware.

title_x: A thin, powerful, and sort of light mobile workstation for creative professionals with some flaws
text:
The FusionTech Sharp 5750 is the version of the more consumer-focused ABC 17 targeted towards professionals in the creative field that want a relatively (keyword being relatively) thin and light laptop with high CPU and moderate GPU performance. While there are thinner and lighter 17" laptops, and higher performing (but heavier and bigger) laptops, the Sharp 5750 attempts to balance the two. It certainly hits its targets in a lot of ways, but misses in many ways too.

My particular model is what I would call moderately spec'd. Unlike many reviews you'll see on this model, mine has the mid-range CPU, a 10th generation i7-10750H, a 6-core, 12-thread CPU at 2.60ghz with up to 5.0ghz turbo boost, the Nvidia Quadro RTX 3000 Max-Q with 6gb of VRAM, 32gb of RAM, and a 512gb "Class 40" SSD. This comes with a 1-year basic warranty that includes on-site service.

For me, this provides more performance than my previous laptop, a FusionTech Sharp 7510, with a bigger screen and lower weight. This is significantly faster at things like 3D rendering with Blender and video encoding.

Here's my conclusion, if you don't want to read the rest of this review: this is a very nice laptop that straddles the line between performance and portability with very nice build quality and features, and I really do like mine. However, due to its similarities to the ABC 17, I can really only recommend the Sharp 5750 to professionals that need the configurations offered only on the Sharp line; most people would be served just as well by the ABC 17 that comes in at a lower price point. I don't think this particular configuration of the Sharp 5750 makes much sense -- I would suggest going up to an 8-core CPU (i7-10875H, i9-10885H, or the Xeon W-10885M) and a 1TB SSD.

PROS
👍 Big, beautiful screen with very thin bezels
👍 "Relatively" thin and light for a 17" laptop
👍 Fast performance
👍 Great build quality
👍 Nice keyboard and trackpad feel

CONS
👎 Expensive, even compared with the nearly identical ABC 17
👎 Thermal throttling under high load
👎 Difficult to open for servicing
👎 512gb SSD is limiting for the target audience of content creators
👎 Should include an 8-core CPU at this price
👎 Only 1 year basic warranty is poor for a "professional" machine at this price point

PHYSICAL
This is the thin and light 17" mobile workstation in FusionTech's precision line. At about 5.5 lbs, it's not the lightest 17" laptop, but it's definitely lighter than the nearly 7lb FusionTech Sharp 7750. Due to the incredibly thin bezels for the screen, this laptop is actually slightly smaller than my previous laptop, a 15" FusionTech Sharp 7510. The build quality is very, very nice -- the laptop is very rigid, the screen is also rigid, looking around the edge of the laptop everything lines up. The bottom case of the laptop is some kind of metal alloy; the edges are finished nicely. The laptop lid is a matt gray metal alloy, and the keyboard deck and palm rest look like carbon fiber.

The bottom panel can be removed for upgrading the storage and RAM by removing 8 torx screws and then prying the bottom panel off. The bottom panel, after removing the screws, is held in very tightly by clips, and it required a lot of force to remove (I actually broke one of the clips). Inside, you'll find the two easily accessible RAM slots and 2 NVME slots for SSDs. To install or remove an SSD, you have to disconnect and remove the battery. I successfully added a 2nd 1TB SSD.

Replacing anything other than the storage, RAM, and battery will be difficult. Replacing the keyboard, for example, requires taking out EVERYTHING and then you have to replace the entire top case.

This has 4 Thunderbolt 3/USB C ports, a combo headphone/mic jack, and a full-size SD card slot. The SD card slot isn't spring loaded, you just insert the SD card (which only goes in half way) and pull it out. I would have liked at least a single USB A port, and a normal DC in port would have allowed the use of a more powerful adapter that would have eliminated the power limit noted below.

SCREEN
The screen is one of the best attributes of this laptop. This is a 17", 16:10, 3840x2400 display supporting 500 nits, 100% Adobe RGB, HDR400, and 10-bit color. This display also supports touch and is covered with anti-reflective Gorilla glass. The display looks well-calibrated to my eye. FusionTech uses their PremierColor app to allow you to change the color space between native, sRGB, AdobeRGB, DCI-P3, Rec. 709, and others that are less useful. This is easily the best laptop display I've used, it looks just as good as the LG Ultrafine 5k in my office. I run this with 200% scaling and everything looks very sharp.

The screen is limited in recline to maybe 135 degrees due to the hinge design. I would have liked a bit more recline, but this is fine for most situations. There is an ambient light sensor which can adjust the brightness of the display based on your environment.

KEYBOARD & TRACKPAD
Keyboard is great to type on. Although it's different from my previous FusionTech Sharp 7510 with slightly less travel, it still has sufficient travel and a nice positive engagement. The trackpad on this laptop is huge -- there's no buttons, but you can click on the bottom edge, but I prefer to use tap to click. The usual gestures work. I have noticed a few situations where it doesn't track my fingers well, but that happens sporadically and may be due to something about my environment; I'll update once I do more testing.

Another observation: I'm not sure if this is only for my particular sample, but the keyboard/palmrest is not 100% flat -- putting a ruler against the palmrest, there's some areas that are maybe 0.5 mm high or low. It doesn't seem to affect either the typing experience or the screen when closed.

PERFORMANCE
On to the performance, one of the defining attributes of this laptop. This particular configuration of the laptop has a 6-core 10th generation Core i7 processor, 32 gb of DDR4 ram running at 2933 mhz, and the Nvidia Quadro RTX 3000 Max-Q. Subjectively it's fast, but here's a few benchmarks (done with FusionTech's Power Manager set to Ultra Performance):
🧪 Cinebench R23: 1124 single, 7422 when on ultra performance
🧪 Blender benchmark: CUDA - 42m 20s, CPU 1hr23m14s
🧪 FFXV Benchmark: 7900
🧪 UserBenchmark: Gaming 63%, Desktop 90%, Workstation 58%

Due to the thinness of this laptop, it will thermal throttle given a long, heavy workload. Cinebench multicore would start to thermal throttle after maybe 2 or 3 minutes. The 130W power adapter is also not capable of supplying enough power if you are maxing out both the CPU and GPU; it will start to draw from the battery. If you are running workloads such as this regularly, you might want to step up to the Sharp 7550 or 7750.

This has two fans. When just browsing the web, the fans don't spin up at all. Most of the time the fans are barely audible, but when under load you can hear them. I don't find the sound annoying, but it is very noticeable -- it sounds like a lot of wind mixed with a bit of fan whine.

The fan intakes are along the bottom with the exhaust in the hinge area. The bottom case has a ridge near the hinge that rises the rear of the laptop up, both for improved ventilation and to provide a slightly tilted keyboard surface, but it's only a few mm. You will likely want some kind of laptop stand to further lift the laptop up to improve the ventilation.

FusionTech SOFTWARE
One of the great things about the Sharp line is the FusionTech software. This comes pre-installed with FusionTech SupportAssist, Power Manager, PremierColor, and Optimizer. SupportAssist provides diagnostics and driver updates, Power Manager allows you to set charging thresholds and adjust the thermal configuration to optimize performance or reduce noise, and I mentioned PremierColor in the Screen section. The FusionTech Optimizer app consolidates a few different settings into a single app, including audio settings, power settings, and settings for the proximity sensor -- this will lock and unlock your laptop when you walk away and come back.

The FusionTech BIOS and recovery software is also quite nice. All the screens are graphical, such as the BIOS and the Boot Menu. There is an embedded version of SupportAssist for OS recovery, and it has the quite cool feature of having an embedded web browser that will allow you to look up your Bitlocker key if you need it.

Other than this FusionTech software, there's no other bloatware.

OTHER
This includes a webcam with IR, which you can use for facial recognition with Windows Hello. The webcam is only 720p and is OK, but not great for video conferencing. It's a bit grainy and doesn't do well with low-light. This also has a fingerprint reader built into the top of the power button.

This includes a single combined USB-C to USB-A and HDMI adapter.

You will probably want to get a Thunderbolt 3 dock if you don't already have one. Only FusionTech docks can provide 130W of power over the Thunderbolt port to FusionTech laptops, which you may need when doing anything intensive. FusionTech suggests a WD19TB; I am using an older model dock, the TB16, without any issues so far.

BATTERY LIFE
This configuration includes a 97 Wh battery. For typical usage (web browser, email, productivity apps), in my preliminary testing, I would expect 8-9 hours. I expect this will drop significantly when doing anything intensive.

CONCLUSION
The FusionTech Sharp 5750 is an amazing piece of technology, with great build quality in a package that provides a lot of performance in a relatively thin and light package. It does have flaws -- the performance is ultimately limited by the form factor, with thermal throttling in extended heavy workloads, and it's not as maintainable as its bigger siblings. This only has USB C ports, when it there is room for at least one USB A port. It is very similar to the ABC 17, to the point where consumers and anybody that doesn't need the higher end configurations only available on the Sharp will be better served by the ABC 17. However, if you use your laptop professionally, the additional options and support offered by the Sharp line will be appealing.

UPDATES
After 1 month of use: I have noticed that the trackpad will sometimes stop responding for a second or two randomly -- it seems to be driver-related though, as I don't really experience the issue in Linux.

Battery life with light usage is about 8 hours.

I tried to contact FusionTech to discuss other warranty options, but they never replied to my inquiry.

Temperatures are pretty low when doing web browsing and light coding (VS code/Javascript) -- most of the time the fans don't turn on.

UPDATE 2 (8/2021)
The successor to this laptop, the FusionTech Sharp 5760, has been released. It shares the same chassis as this model, so many of my comments will still apply. The 5760 has 11th gen Intel CPUs and an Nvidia RTX 3060 equivalent (the RTX A2000). These combined will give you a noticeable boost in performance, so I would recommend that you look to the newer model if it's not much more than this 5750.

text:
The Advance m15...not your daddy's corporate windows laptop. This has all the best specs to play all the newest games that your grandma's laptop won't play...

Advance builds gamer laptops. For those that don't know, FusionTech bough Advance some time back but they are still cranking out their specialty laptops...

What I like:
++The Best Tech to run all the latest stuff. This laptop costs so much because it has all the best (ie, most expensive) tech. Top CPU, top CPU, top DRAM, top gaming HD screen, etc.

++Good brand. Advance has always been held in esteem. Not sure if FusionTech owning has diminished the luster but Advance definitely knows how to put together gamer laptops and all that goes along with it (the screen refresh rates, the fan cooling, etc).

++The quality and coolness. Feels good and well built, looks cool with the LED lights, etc.

What could be better:
--The BATTERY LIFE. This is known and not a strength of gamer laptops. I get about 60-90 minutes batter life on this Advance m15. So this is not a couchsurfer of coffee shop email reader. The battery is most handy as safety backup for power outages, etc.

--The fan noise. The latest tech specs use lots of power so this Advance laptop uses lots of power. This requires extra cooling and there are extra fans for this, etc. ie, lots of fans always buzzing and comes with the territory.

Overall, it's an Advance and it is cool. At current price of $2400 it is pricey. It would be more versatile for me if the battery life was longer. But, has all the best tech specs and works well to play all the latest software. You don't need this if you using your PC for just the basics. Overall 4-STAR rating by me in consideration of price/value.

title_x: Separate GPU and UHD, Nice.  Less nice: 64GB Max & TBird Hub Experience
text:
The 5750 model is a hefty laptop which IMHO is intended to bring a separate GPU capability (vs a built-in Intel GPU device, more commonly embedded) to an enterprise-grade laptop. You also get UHD resolution, which is an excellent advance over HD.

FusionTech achieves this with, in my testing, a solid-forming machine that shines when running applications that need that GPU.

My most serious concerns about this machine are related to the Thunderbolt hub subsystem. This hardware / firmware combination promises a lot, and delivers on a fair amount of that goal. For instance, the design offers higher speed alternatives to the old docking station design, such as additional video ports and charging ports. But these benefits come with some, in my testing with this model and with other FusionTech laptops (I regularly use a FusionTech ABC 15 and a Latitude 5411) limitations. These limitations are mostly instabilities.

For instance, while devices plugged into the TB hub (vs. directly to the laptop) should support hot plug actions. But I found that some devices (e.g., a USB keyboard) could not be recognized without a reboot -- a nuisance -- but not every time the device is used.

Also, while the Thunderbolt interface is fast, it seemed sensitive to some disruptive interactions across devices, especially when for instance the USB-C port is used to support an external HD monitor.

I also found that the FusionTech Management tooling, intended to keep the firmware current, etc., didn't always run properly / at all. These occasional failures put a worry line on my brow.

POSSIBLE DEAL-BREAKER

And last, and worst, the 64GB DDR4 maximum is a potential deal-breaker. (SOURCE Crucial wizard).

These nits might not be important if it were not for this laptop's striving to be relatively top tier.

PRICING
This is a not inexpensive machine, even with typical Amazon pricing discounting. That there is only 32GB and an SSD with only 512GB (starting swap space alone will use a bunch of it) are limitations that I wouldn't want to live with in an ideal configuration.

Also, for pro mobility, I would like to have RAID 1. Backing up a complex Win 10 environment is possible with third party solutions, but they mean carrying more stuff with you. Yes, SSD's can fail, at least in the sense that they become unbootable to Windows.

TIP
Look out for third party AC => DC adapters. This machine needs a beefy power supply and will complain and might not work at all if you try to use something less.

I also think that the price point as listed on Amazon is somewhat high considering the particular configuration tested. Since aftermarket expandability of laptops today is increasingly limited, you are forced to decide ahead of time what you'll need.

text:
-3 YEARS AFTER PURCHASE (June 2018)
TL:DR: Recurring issues with overheating(common with this model) and poor customer service from FusionTech.

Since I bought it I've had a time where the laptop overheated (85+ degrees Celcius) and fried the motherboard while playing OW in the lowest settings. It may not pertain to everyone, but I had to send my laptop back to FusionTech Headquarters in Texas 4 times, each time taking over a week and the computer still came back faulty every time. Also, I had to pay for shipping each time. Recently, the computer couldn't even open a game or a few chrome tabs before the fans sounded like an F-18 was flying around my room. When I say it couldn't do anything, I really mean it - before it got to that point, I would be playing a game(like rocket league and Apex Legends) on minimum settings until there were consistent 5-20 second frame drops (1-10 FPS), and all games became basically unplayable. After extensive research, I found out that many users that bought this laptop also consistently have issues with overheating. The complete laptop teardown necessary for a repasting seemed overwhelming to me, a person who has never worked on a modern-day laptop, so I decided to take it into a shop to get it fixed for around $100. What me and my friends (who also have gaming laptops) learned the hard way is that unless you absolutely need portability, always opt for a desktop. I know I'm bound to have more overheating issues in the future - and I'll never get a gaming laptop again.

title_x: A Portable Next-Gen Console of a Laptop
text:
With GPUs being in short supply these days, gaming laptops may be the new way gamers get to enjoy their favorite games. I guess the miners arent using gaming laptops to do their crypto stuff.

My particular model of the Advance m15 r4 came with a Intel Core i7-10870H and a RTX 3070. In Geekbench 5, this laptop scored a 1254 on the single core score and 7026 on the multicore score. The video card scored 132987 on CUDA, 117718 on OpenCL, and 72857 on Vulkan. These are the best video card device scores I have ever seen in any of my devices. I think the CPU scores are a little disappointing though.

This model has 16GB or RAM, which I condsider the sweet spot for Windows 10 for price and performance.
The white body of the laptop is an off-white color. When paired with my Razer Deathaddder white mouse, you can see a difference in the shade of white, but they do look nice together.

The laptop features RGB backlighting under the keys and also around the backside of the laptop. Speaking of the backside, this laptop has a weird shape to it, that only photos can accurately convey. It almost looks like a rounded-rectangle exhaust port on an alien ship. I guess that's what they were going for.

The keyboard is not the new-fangled Cherry mechanical switches. At least, I don't think they are. They sound like membrane keys and have a dull thud when pressed.

The glass trackpad is small, but very nice. The sharp edges of the laptop keyboard deck may bother your wrists after extended playing sessions. I am noticing it just typing this review.

Enabling the performance mode in the Advance Command Center makes the fans sound like a rocket launch.

I am using this laptop in balanced mode, and that was the mode I used for benchmarks as well.

It paired easily with an Xbox controller, that I bought specifically to use with this laptop.

Overall, I am very happy with this laptop and might make the jump to PC gaming instead of getting a new next-gen console.

title_x: Well made workstation, top of it's class! Thinnest smallest workstation on the market.
text:
Very sleek looking amazing machine! Powers on very quickly and runs flawlessly smooth no matter what demanding tasks I'm doing.

Looking at the outer case you'll see a metal shell on the top and bottom with a diamond cut polished edge that results in a stunning sturdy feeling shell! On the inside you see a very classy looking carbon fiber palm rest. You'll also notice they took out the 10 key pad to make room for big speaker panels on each side of the keyboard. The panel is so large because it has a speaker on top and a subwoofer on the bottom which makes for very impressive sound! You definitely won't need to tote around external speakers with this! You can however get a 10 key pad that hooks into one of the 4 usb- c ports. Those ports are all thunderbolt 3 ports which support full native 8k resolution (this is the smallest workstation on the market that has this feature.)

The screen is a gorgeous 17" touch screen UHD+ display that has hardware enabled blue light filtering that doesn't cause that ugly dimming or yellowing that others do. This keeps your graphics looking good while reducing the strain on your eyes and you will absolutely notice the difference! It drastically helps your eyes when you have to work many hours at a time without a break.

Supports Windows Hello so you can use a pin number, fingerprint, or your face to login. The power button in the upper right is unmarked due to it doubling as the fingerprint reader. The facial recognition works thru the IR camera and it can be set to lock your computer the second you walk away from it and unlock it when you come back. Amazing for shared work spaces where you're constantly having to get up and leave your computer- never have to worry about whether you locked it or not! The camera and microphone built in are impressive- I've done Skype video calls and Zoom meetings and gotten flawless results without even needing an external microphone! The camera produces a very smooth video feed that isn't ever choppy as long as you have a good reliable internet that's high speed.

If you're wondering about the price tag, it's because this isn't a laptop- it's workstation. This is more made for things like high end video work, medical imaging, architectural work, 3D CAD, graphic design, animation, AI, and VR (this is also the smallest workstation on the market that is VR capable.) As for video editing- I'm VERY impressed. You get very smooth playback while editing 4k videos and can do it in much less time than other workstations- extremely impressive!

If you're worried about it overheating while you're running more demanding tasks and multitasking- it has metal and copper channels inside of it that help the dual output fans cool it and push hot air thru the system and out the back which keeps this thing running cool! I've yet to see mine begin to overheat while I'm running demanding programs and really pushing it.

Working from home and on the go- this is absolutely your perfect solution and the best workstation on the market in my opinion! I'm just blown away by this impressive powerhouse of a workstation! FusionTech really took my breath away with how well built this is and how jam packed with tech it is. I could tell you about the tech in it all day long but I'll leave the rest for you to research on your own. It suffices to say- this is a workstation that can handle quite the work load and not begin to get weighed down in the process, total game changer!! This is definitely the one you've been looking for!

title_x: Very powerful, very nice, very expensive
text:
This is a professional class workstation level system. This is not that heavy, but a 17 inch plus laptop is not something you want to move very often if you can help it. The size of the power brick and screen make this a much better desktop model than the sit on the couch model.

This particular model I am reviewing has 32 gb of main system memory, an RTX 3000 quadro GPU with 6 gb of video memory, and a 4k IGZO UHD screen in a 16 by 10 aspect ratio. It has 4 thunderbolt ports and it does not mess around.

This has the same or very similar footprint to a FusionTech ABC 17 inch, so carbon fiber aspects, good quality keyboard. Speakers are not the loudest I've heard, but very excellent stereo separation and very good depth. And pretty loud, just perhaps not as loud as a peak apple MacBook pro or MacBook air.

This is a pro laptop for professional graphics/cad work and it is pretty good for that. I will say, you pay a lot for the FusionTech name and the form factor. And the 4k plus screen.

My main concern is just the price--if you need a laptop for a workstation this is a solid choice. It is no longer state of the art given it has a 2.6 core i7 10th gen intel processor, which is kind of smoked by the AMD models or the newer 11th gen products. But, perhaps it can be a solid value for the right price.

Of course, if you could find the parts, a comparable desktop would likely be a lot more powerful.

Despite the 32 gb memory, it only has a 512 gb storage drive--I guess they assume you are using network storage or will use something attached to a thunderbolt port. For the price at least a 1 TB nvme drive would be more appropriate.

Overall a solid machine for those that need workstation level performance in a semi-portable form factor and amazing screen. But this kind of hardware certainly comes at a high price premium. If you have other options, most will be much cheaper, although not necessarily better.

text:
So, instead of going into benchmarks, recaps of all the ports, and all that other stuff, I'm going to jump right in and talk about real-world use of this thing, because that's what really matters. Most people aren't going to tweak it carefully to get every a few more FPS out of it, and frankly, I'm not a competitive gamer or Twitch streamer or Youtuber. I'm a gamer who likes to actually play games instead of fussing with overclocking and benchmarks.

So how does it do out of the box?

The answer, you'll be happy to know, is very well indeed. Fast. In fact, the screen refresh and speed was TOO high for Fallout 4 and I needed to install a mod (high FPS fix) to make the game playable because without it everything was flying at super speed. Other, more modern games fared better in that regard, and pretty much everything I have thrown at it plays beautifully on high or ultra settings at 1080p with frame rates well above 60 FPS on the 300Hz screen. Rest assured, when it comes to gaming this thing can handle anything you throw at it up to and including games released in 2021. My favorite is an older title-- Skyrim-- but I run with a TON of mods including 4k textures, tons of new actors, and improved lighting and weather effects, and this thing crunches all of that like it's nothing. I've never seen the game looking so amazing, so smooth, or so full. On the other hand, if you want to try something newer like Cyberpunk 2077, you'll be happy to see this uses all the latest tricks. DLSS, Ambient occlusion, ray tracing... The works. You'll cry, it looks so good.

The screen, by the way, is gorgeous. Yes, it's 'only' 1080p resolution, but the 300Hz refresh rate is out of this world and the colors pop. It's beautiful, and it makes me kind of glad this isn't a touch screen model because frankly, it would be a shame to get fingerprints on that screen!

The body is aluminum. It's smooth, sleek, and cool (temperature-wise, but also socially speaking). The LED lights are a nice touch, and they're fully customizable via the My Advance app. The system comes with no bloatware, thank goodness, except for the usual Windows 10 stuff like Skype, Office 365 trial, and some games that are all easily uninstalled.

I have also added extra storage, which was extremely easy. Remove the bottom panel (several screws, including some that are 'capture screws' that you should know Do Not Come Out, but are designed to stay in the housing so you don't lose them) and then slot in your own M.2 in the available slot. There are actually two M.2 slots, but one is a weird small sized one that, from what I've seen, is nearly impossible to find for any decent price at this point in time. Still, I was able to add an additional 500GB to the included 1TB, and that's plenty of space for a gaming laptop.

Let's talk about the keyboard: It's REALLY nice. It has a sort of mechanical feel. The keys have decent travel and give feedback, but they're not too loud. Of course it's backlit (and customizable) and there are no surprises like power buttons where the Delete key should be (you designers know who I'm talking about). All in all, if this wasn't a gaming laptop it would be an incredibly fine laptop for writing and doing office work.

The sound is equally impressive. I couldn't believe the near-surround effect it provides, along with the rich sound, from small laptop speakers. In terms of sound this blows away any laptop I've had, and I've had everything from high-end VAIOs to Microsoft Surface to MacBook Pros. The sound on this beats them as far as I'm concerned. Again, this is clearly made to be a gaming laptop and it shows.

Now, the downside of all this: Heat. Anything you do that taxes the system even a little will kick in the fans on the normal setting. You can make it run in a quiet mode (and then it runs hot) or in a cool mode (and then it runs loud), but the bottom line is that you're rocking a new i7 and a GeForce RTX 3070 in this thing, and those are going to produce some heat. I highly suggest a cooling pad of some sort, even though the fans on the laptop can handle the heat. It's always nice to cut down the risk and extend the life of your laptop by keeping it cool and happy.

And for all that power, it's pretty darn lightweight although you'll find the power brick to be another story. It's a big beast that gives you the wattage required for top-tier gaming, but will definitely take up some space in your laptop bag. I suggest a BIG bag with separate compartments, because you'll want this big brick well away from the screen on your laptop.

So yeah, there are trade-offs, but at the end of the day the point of a gaming laptop is POWER, and this has it to spare. Connect to a nice monitor and sound system and you have a gaming laptop that can rival most gaming desktops. Even without the monitor and external sound, you have a solid gaming system here that will impress you and keep you gaming for a long time to come.

So it's without any hesitation that I give this Advance masterpiece of a laptop five glowing stars. Bravo!
