title_x: FusionTech premier line at its finest...
text:
Arriving inside a classic FusionTech box (we all know the look), inside is a very elegant presentation in a nice black box that is magnatized and opens up to reveal the FusionTech ABC 9710. Inside, you get the laptop, USB-C power adapter, power cord and a neat little FusionTech branded dongle along with some instructions. Minimalist in the best way.

Once you take an initial look at this beautiful laptop, you quickly realize this is clearly FusionTech's answer to Apple's 16" Macbook Pro in the BEST way possible.

It has a very high build quality. The backlit keyboard, which eschews the number pad, is perfectly centered with decent speakers on each side. Like Apple, the trackpad is extremely oversized and responds to both taps and clicks along with various gestures. The display is 3840x2400 vs the standard 3840x2160 to even match the Mac's 16:10 ratio versus others 16:9. It even mimics the dual thunderbolt ports on each side and is powered by a compact(ish) USB-C power brick. FusionTech includes an adorable little dongle that has a single USB-A port and HDMI out, but of course the beauty of standard Thunderbolt ports is you can dongle your way to just about any type of connectivity you desire.

Weighing in at ~5lbs 7oz, it is deceptively solid and depending on what you're used to using, it will feel slightly heavier or lighter. I normally use large laptops that use desktop processors or massive gaming laptops so I'm used to heaving around 11lb+ units with 3-4lb power supplies so this solidly built laptop feels relatively light. On the other hand, I have a few 15.6" and 14" Acers that are well under 5lbs, so compared to those it feels a touch heavy. Still, with everything included weighing a total of 6lbs 7oz, it is very manageable to move around and use.

Powered by an Intel i7-11800h 11th gen 10nm processor, this is the optimal selection for this laptop. Do not feel any buyer's remorse for skipping the i9-11900h or i9-11980hk as all three (i7-11800h, i9-11900k and i9-11980hk) are 8 core, 16 thread CPUs and thermal constraints will effectively make them all equal in system performance as they each run up against the inherent system power and thermal limits even with the advanced vapor chamber cooling FusionTech has implemented. Save yourself a very large chunk of money and pick the i7-11800h as it will perform effectively the same as the other two, pricier options.

The 512GB M.2 NVMe is very speedy with another M.2 bay open and powered by dual channel 3200 16GB (2x8GB) memory, you are good to go right out of the box for your Windows 10 Pro needs. Luckily, the memory and storage are fully upgradeable so you can adjust it to your requirements. For those of you who are wondering what type of memory density ships with the ABC 9710, unfortunately it is the inferior 1Rx16 and not the superior 1Rx8 so if you want to carve out a little bit more performance from your system you can swap to 1Rx8 at your discretion.

First time starting up you're met with all the standard setup options to get you up and running. This is a great and easy way to auto register your system with FusionTech for their award winning warranty service. The first thing you will want to do is a full Windows Update as the sheer amount of updates is massive including a large array of BIOS and FIRMWARE updates that will fix a few fan issues among other things. FusionTech works closely with Microsoft and Intel and it shows as the bulk of the drivers, even specialized ones, are immediately available for update and install making keeping your system up to date very easy.

Depending on what you're using, performance is a mixed bag as the fans are slow to respond and the unit will thermal throttle quickly because the fans take to long to respond. Testing with Cinebench 23, it is a race between getting the cooling up to full speed before the system throttles down permanently to its stock 45w rating. The CPU will initially even want to pull 90w+. Elevating the rear of the unit helps greatly to keep the throttle down to 45w from happening but it will still eventually settle in around 75w and continually bounce off the thermal limits routinely hitting 100 and throttling down. I was able to achieve a max score of 12600 multi and 1522 single which is just amazing for such a light, thin laptop. Even single threaded tests had individual cores hitting in the 90's which is concerning but it did not thermal throttle on single threaded tests so that is a plus. The fans are definitely there when under load but I've heard much louder from much lesser systems. Via the BIOS or FusionTech software, you can pick custom profiles to adjust for cool, quiet or ultra performance. But keeping everything in perspective, the overall performance was great and more than acceptable.

The 3840x2400 16:10 display is absolutely gorgeous....jaw dropping so and you can see it is the centerpiece of this high end laptop. 17.3" with insanely bright ratings for a laptop panel (500 nit) and Dolby Vision HDR support along with full 100% sRGB and 100% Adobe coverage, it is a joy to view. Minimal back light bleed and zero bad pixels was the icing on the display cake for my unit. Colors are amazing and it is very responsive for desktop use. It absolutely trounces all my current and previous laptop panels and most of my desktop panels. If you are looking for a top notch screen, this is it.

I found the keyboard to be more than passable and the backlit functionality is great with a very classic FusionTech look. The very spacious track pad is great. Solid to the touch and very responsive. I had no problems whipping all around the screen and using a few gestures for added functionality. Tapping and solid clicks both worked great. If you happen to end up with a bad touch pad as some have reported, reach out to FusionTech's warranty services and they will take care of it. Having used FusionTech Warranty Services numerous times over the past 10-15 years, their service and support is top notch.

The Nvidia RTX 3050 4GB video at first glance is an odd choice. It is woefully under powered to drive the native resolution of 3840x2400 for gaming (Even desktop 3090's are pushed to the max supporting 4k) unless you really dial down the settings. If you opt to run games at 1920x1200 (1:2 ratio), they run much better with a decent level of eye candy on. The panel is only 60hz but that makes sense with this level of GPU option. Basically, it is good enough that if you want to get some gaming done you definitely can but compromises and sacrifices will need to be made to achieve decent frame rates to keep it at or around 60fps depending on your games played. It scored ~9000 in Superposition which is right in line with other 3050 scores and the 3050 itself runs nice and cool. There are other models with a 3060, but in the end this is not a "gaming laptop" but an elegant productivity laptop that can also game if desired....you know....like the Macbook Pros.

The webcam could be better but it gets the job done. This seems to be the issue with most laptops even to this day. It is more than passable but like just about every other laptop out there, if you require much better audio and visual clarity, you will need to purchase an external solution.Wireless is powered by Killer's 1650 and is fast and speedy and adheres to new WiFi 6e standards which is a plus.

Battery life is great. I tend to use my laptops plugged in a large amount of the time but when I needed to use it moving around for various tasks, the battery didn't even get to 25% during the day which was wonderful. I'm sure you can find plenty of "run time" tests out on the Interwebs, but for my use it works great. I would suggest turning off ultra performance and moving to a balanced or battery conservative selection for your power plan.

Overall, I am very pleased with the ABC 9710. I LOVE the screen. It really is the star of the show hands down. The backlit keyboard is great. The track pad is massive and great to use. Performance is more than adequate and the i7-11800h paired with 16gb of dual channel 3200 memory and a very speed 512GB drive is the perfect sweet spot while keeping costs reasonable for this caliber of laptop. The 3050 will allow you to get some gaming in while having access to Nvidia's full array of 3000 series perks and the 4x Thunderbolt ports really let you dongle your system "your way." It is the perfect blend of a full size 17.3" laptop with a decent weight profile, performance and good battery life to not only become your next laptop but also your only computer you will possibly need.

I like it so much that this will be replacing my Acers and former Clevo as my new daily driver and main laptop it is just that good.

5/5

title_x: For the price it's a good deal, but you could do much better...
text:
An RTX 3060 laptop for under $1400 (with $140 discount at the time of purchase) seemed like a good deal but to get to that price point a lot was sacrificed it seems.

Pros:
- Price was affordable
- Build quality is very sturdy. Very little flex in the chassis or screen.
- In-stock. Nearly everything else I wanted was out of stock or price gouged by scalpers
- No dead pixels as far as I can tell.
- Nice speakers but fans can still be heard over them.

Cons:
- TDP of 3060 is only 90 watts. Confirmed with GPU-Z.
- Gets VERY Hot. GPU easily hit 90 degrees Celsius then crashed while gaming from overheating.
- Keyboard is not great. Missed key presses constantly and using red letters on black keys is a terrible idea.
- Mux switch is in the BIOS and can not be changed in Windows
- Bloatware. 512gb SSD but only 407gb free.
- Some backlight bleed. Very noticeable on dark scenes.
- Ships with dead battery. I thought I had a DOA unit cause it would not boot up.
- Color is not black. It's a very dark dirty grey unlike the pictures.

Overall its a nice laptop but I was mislead by reviews online and and the Q&A section that this was the high wattage 3060. Due to the thermal issue I'm guessing that's why they opted for the lower watt version. The cooling could be better IMHO as evidenced by the crashes I experience from overheating. If you can get it on a sale and not MSRP its a better deal than most 3050 ti laptops. It's good enough for basic gaming but don't expect to run modern games on it at high framerates/quality. Despite having a Core i7 CPU I'm constantly experiencing system stuttering which could be a windows issue or caused by all the bloatware. FusionTech did not include any backup disks or a restore option so I can not uninstall anything without losing it forever. I will update my review after the return period is over to see if it holds up.

title_x: Good general use laptop. Quality at a reasonable price
text:
I am using this for one task only; to keep track of the wines in my wine cellar. I say this because I have read that some find this machine running hot; mine is in a 55F environment, so that’s not an issue for me.

I like the look and feel of this laptop; it’s maybe just a tad on the heavy side for a mini-laptop these days, but it feels sturdy, and I’ve had too many bad experiences with super fragile laptops. This laptop is a nice compromise between heft and portability. Don't get me wrong, it's very light and not too thick, but I'm comparing it to other minis out there. The upside is its greater ability to survive abuse.

I do miss a touch screen; I almost expect that in every laptop I buy now. But, on the other hand, the i7 CPU, the 16 GB of RAM, the Nvidia GeForce, and the 2GB GDDR6 are more than I would expect on a laptop, from a reliable brand, at this price.

Although I have this set for a singular task, I always load it with most of the programs that I use so that if my primary laptop breaks, I have another set up for immediate use. This laptop easily handled any of my typical work programs, most MS Office programs, and web browsers, with no problem at all. They all loaded quickly and ran fast.

I like the fingerprint protection, and it helps speed booting up and opening a program. In addition, the power brick is not too large, it and the laptop will fit easily into any computer bag or backpack.

The backlit keyboard is very easy to type on; the keystroke pressure is very light but has good tactile feedback, and finger fatigue will not be an issue.

One little touch that I really enjoy is the camera shutter, a small built-in slide to cover the lens. And, as the world is moving towards type-C USBs, It’s good to see two of them here as well as a type A. The built-in HDMI port is also great since I usually work with two monitors.

I’ve had many FusionTech computers, and I think of them as very reliable and, when an issue occurs, I’ve experienced good customer service. That would make me recommend this laptop for home, school, and office use as long as it’s not used for intensive tasks such as gaming or memory-intensive graphic applications.

title_x: Good laptop for creative work and occasional gaming, with some minor caveats
text:
The Worktop 16 has a lot going for it, but a few shortcomings keep it from being perfect. The laptop’s strengths include a great screen, strong CPU performance, fast storage, and a responsive keyboard. However, the laptop isn’t ideal for gaming, its SD card reader is sluggish, and on my unit, the touchpad curls up at two corners. This laptop could be a great choice for content creators, but frequent gamers probably should look elsewhere.

The 3K-resolution screen is what really drew me to this laptop, and it doesn’t disappoint. Everything looks razor-sharp, colors are accurate, and the 16:10 aspect ratio is great for keeping extra toolbars/timeline on-screen while editing. The screen does have some backlight bleed along the top and bottom edges, but generally it shouldn’t be an issue unless you frequently work with very dark content.

Performance from the i7-11800H CPU is excellent, and this laptop handles everything I throw at it with ease. The 512GB NVMe SSD also does well, with read/write speeds around 3500/2500 MB/s, which is great for a PCIe 3.0-based drive. On the flip side, the laptop’s built-in SD card slot is a disappointment. For some reason, FusionTech installed an antiquated USB 2.0-based reader, which offers a maximum transfer rate of just 30 MB/s. If you frequently handle photos/videos by SD card, you’ll definitely want to use your own USB 3.x card reader instead of the laptop’s SD card slot.

When it comes to graphics performance, the 65W RTX 3050 GPU serves well for most creative applications but can feel underwhelming in video games. The screen’s native 3K resolution is a lot to ask of this lower-end GPU, so gamers would be best off connecting an external 1080p monitor for better results. On a positive note, the laptop’s GPU comes with Resizable BAR support already enabled, which provides a small boost in some games.

Build quality of the laptop is generally good, with one exception on the unit I received. On my laptop, the touchpad has a warping problem that makes it curl at the upper corners. The touchpad is attached by double-sided tape, which hasn’t been holding up over time, so I have to press the corners back down before using the laptop. I’m sure FusionTech would fix it under warranty, but it’s a mostly cosmetic issue that hasn’t yet annoyed me enough to ship the laptop in for service.

Touchpad aside, the rest of the hardware is solid. The keyboard feels responsive, with moderately-short travel, although its white-only backlighting could be brighter (lighting choices are dim, very dim, and off). The laptop offers decent upgrade potential, which is somewhat uncommon nowadays in mainstream consumer devices. RAM, SSD, and WiFi are provided as slotted cards for easy replacement (with a spare 2230 SSD heatsink included, which was a nice surprise).

Overall, the Worktop 16 is a powerful laptop that hits most of the right notes for content creation and general-purpose computing, but heavy gamers will likely want for better graphics performance. My only significant complaints are the outdated SD card reader and warped touchpad (the latter of which could be an isolated case on my unit). Four stars.

text:
The FusionTech ABC 17 is probably one of the best, Windows based, personal laptop computers that you can buy, there are some many things that FusionTech did right with this generation of the ABC 17, and at the same time there are so many things that they missed and could have done much better.
Let me start by listing all the positives and the features I absolutely love about this model:

- Excellent build quality, the chases, the screen, the keyboard, everything is on a apple level of quality, if not even better in some cases, for example the chases feels heavier and more solid.
- Screen size and quality - yes, being able to fit a 17 inch screen in a 15 inch frame, sort of speak, is quite incredible, the screen is plenty bright with 400 nits, the resolution at 4K is good, but only if you are a content creator, about that a little bit more later, and last there is touch for those that like that feature on a laptop, personally I am not a fan.
- Top level CPU combined with a great nVidia RTX2060 MaxQ - now here we have indeed a great CPU represented by the Intel Core I9 10885H with 8 cores and 16 threads, this CPU can deliver a great productivity and is a very capable gaming chip as well. The RTX2060 MaxQ is also still a very good mobile GPU and is great for video rendering and games as well, but about that a bit later.
- Keyboard and touchpad - To me this keyboard and touchpad are one of the best I have used in the last few years, despite the fact that the keyboard is not full size with the numeric pad on the side, it is still very responsive and comfortable to type on, and the touchpad, well is huge and that is convenient. Previous years and versions had an issue with the touchpad being wobbly, but this later version is perfect.
- Four Thunderbolt 3 ports, an SD card and 3.5mm headphone jack on board, TB3 to HDMI and USB-A adapter in the package as well, great port selection and all you need for your content creation.
- 32GB Ram and 1TB fast Nvme of internal storage - top level components that can get you started with your content creation, video editing and everything else.
- Included separate fingerprint sensor for easy access and Windows Hello.

Negatives:

- The cooling system on board is not capable to effectively dissipate the temperatures produced by the CPU and the GPU - I was forced to disable the Turbo Boost in the bios in order to keep the temps in control, otherwise even the simple tasks were making the whole system heat up fast and the CPU temps were going over 100C almost all the time (and that is with 22-23C room temperature) causing the CPU to throttle. With the TB disabled, the temps were around 80C.
- 4K screen - While great for content creation and media consumption, pushing all those pixels can be challenging for the RTX2060 MaxQ, so gaming is almost impossible, unless you are willing to lower all game settings to the minimum possible. otherwise you are looking at 20-25 frames.
- Touch screen, maybe is just my personal preference, but not all laptops need to have touch, especially high-level production or gaming laptops.
- Battery life - obviously with such powerful components inside, the battery life is expected to be nothing amazing, but I was disappointed. Luckily most of the times I am not using the laptop plugged in as a desktop replacement work horse.
- Very expensive, and not only as a laptop, but computer in general. For the price of over $3K you can buy components to build an incredible desktop, even with the component crisis today, same goes for laptops, you can get a top level gaming laptop that can do everything you want.
- Having to use the included TB3 to HDMI adapter in order to output easily on a external screen.
- The included web camera on the screen doesn't match the price tag of the laptop, the quality is poor and for this price, it should have been at least a 2K camera with good quality.
- Because of the poor cooling solution, which btw even with repasting with good Thermal Grizzly past is not improving too much, you can really utilize the potential of all the top-level components.

Overall, despite of the high-quality components and a build quality, it’s really hard to recommend this laptop, I think for the price, you would have a lot more and better choices.

title_x: FusionTech ABC is universally well reviewed, but still has its issues
text:
Super thin, huge 17" touch screen with colors that just POP, large touchpad mouse, and silent chiclet keyboard. These are just the initial impressions one would see at first blush when approaching this high-quality laptop. Look a little deeper and one would find that this FusionTech ABC 17 sports a powerful 11th generation I7-11800H cpu with a dedicated RTX 3050 graphics card with Nvidia's real-time ray tracing and 16gb of ram. A 512GB ssd rounds out the entire package.

The FusionTech ABC 17 is simply elegant and high-quality. I was able to upgrade this laptop to Windows 11 painlessly and the new UI just looks great on this screen. It runs silently during normal web browsing and video watching. When playing games, the fan kicks in and the cooling seems adequate, but I still have an external laptop cooler helping it along.

Speaking of games, this laptop will run the latest games, but being at the bottom of the RTX line of graphics cards, the screen's 3840x2400 resolution simply is too much for the 3050 to run at the highest quality. It means that one would either run at a lower resolution or lower quality. The resolution issue can be alleviated if one turns on DLSS for resolution scaling.

So that is one of the first problems I would point out with the specs that I have in this laptop. The RTX3050 paired with the super high resolution means one must compromise in some way. In addition, performance in VR is somewhat poor. Half Life: Alyx runs well at low quality settings but any higher and the screen stutters and can cause nausea -- this was tested through wired and wireless configurations.

The second complaint that I have for this laptop is that the only included ports are 4 usb Type-C ports, headphone jack and an SD card reader. It is great that the ports support up to Thunderbolt 3, but the fact that no Type-A ports are available, dongles will be a part of life. It's nice that FusionTech includes a dongle that sports an HDMI and a Type-A port, there is no ethernet or display port support out of the box.

A good 9-in-1 dongle will cost you at least $60 and even then, the quality could be questionable. I happened to have a 9-in-1 dongle, but the ethernet port seems to lose connection constantly. This means that either you take a chance with a $60 no-name dongle or you spend over $100 for a proven one.

This then brings me to the last problem that I want to point out. A gaming PC has very high power requirements. Currently, there is no Type-C product that will provide (or pass through) the 130W that the FusionTech ABC 17 will require. It means that the nifty dock that you bought to get the additional ports that you need? It won't be able to power the laptop. You can connect a 100W charger to the laptop, but you will get a warning from the operating system. So perhaps on travel, one can get away with trickle charging the laptop, but at home, you will always be stuck with taking up two ports, one for power and one for your monitor.

Overall, this is a GREAT laptop with high quality build, but at the current specs, some things just cause awkward situations that one needs to work around.

title_x: FusionTech ABC 17 9710: Beauty and Beast in a portable 17 inch laptop.
text:
The FusionTech ABC 17 9710 is a sleek productivity laptop, that looks good and feel fantastic.
The 4k anti-reflective 500-Nit touchscreen is beautiful and bright with excellent color accuracy. It reached 100% sRGB, 100% aRGB, 100% NTSC and 96% DCI-P3.
The display calibration was juts fine out of the box and calibrating just helps with

The laptop is build into an aluminum chassis (common in the ABC line), with a carbon fiber trackpad.

The trackpad is very good, one of the best on a Windows laptop, but it is uneven by a hair. If you are keen to details, and at this price you should be, you will notice that it does requires a longer press and travel on the right side than the left.

The keyboard is comfortable to type and the keys have a nice travel. I like the lack on numpad, which gives space for larger speakers and better sound.
The power button has an integrated fingerprint reader, which makes a faster signing into Windows.

There are 4 Thunderbolt 4 USB C ports (two on each side), headphone jack and a SD card reader. There is an USB C adapter include with an USB A and HDMI port, since the laptop has neither.
If you transfer data from SD cards, you will like the speed, since transferring gigabytes of files takes just seconds.

There is a Windows Hello 720 webcam. Most laptops webcams are disappointing and the 720p webcam here is not exception. I see a lot of folks complaining about laptop webcams quality when filming with huge expensive cameras.
We want slim laptops but good quality webcams and that's not going to happen anytime soon. That is why even smartphones require a bump to be able to fit better quality cameras.

Included a 130W AC to USB C charging adapter. I have several USB C power adapters and I was able to charge the laptop without problems. My USB C adapters are 3x smaller, which make them a better option to travel.
The laptop comes with a huge 97Wh battery, that could last the whole day (8h) for web browsing and light tasks...if you disable the dedicated graphics card and tune down brightness below 50%.
But it could last just a couple of hours depending of the workload.
If you leave on its default setting, it uses Optimus to decided the best power usage.
It takes more than 2 hours to fully charge the battery with the included 130W USB C power adapter.

The Intel Core i7-11800H churns to every task like a champ.

There are two NVMe M.2 slots in case you want to use multimedia content right on the laptop, or just want to have your entire app or game collection on your laptop.
The 512GB Micron 2300 NVMe SSD reach above 3100 read and 2600 MB/s writes speeds while transferring data and it got better marks on CrystalDiskMark speed bench.

The 16GB DDR4 3200MHz RAM is upgradable, so if your work requires more RAM, just remove the bottom cover and have at it. I do praise FusionTech for allowing us, end users, the option to expand the memory on the FusionTech ABC 17 9710 so it will have a longer life.

There is a Killer Wi-Fi 6 AX1650 (2x2) and Bluetooth 5.1. The Wi-Fi 6 might allow us to finally ditch the Ethernet cable. I was able to get 856 Mbit/s download speeds.

The sound is quit nice for a laptop. FusionTech SPX 17 includes a quad speakers setting with a couple firing up on each side of the keyboard and two more firing down on each side of the trackpad (right next to the battery).

The FusionTech ABC 17 9710 is a great laptop for content creation and it does a bit of gaming as well.
The cooling chamber system does a very good job keeping the Core i7-11800H and the RTX 3050 churning along without missing a bit.
The fan wasn't loud when light gaming or light multimedia tasks (31 dB) but it ramps up (49dB) on heavy workloads when the CPU and GPU are taxed.
The palmrest gets a bit warm and it gets pretty toasty around the firs row of the keyboard.

Besides the trackpad right corner issue, I have not found anything else to complain about the FusionTech ABC 17. By the way, this should not be happening on FusionTech's top of the line laptop and quality control (QC) should be better.

I would have like a better webcam and the option of a dark grey color, instead of silver.

Installed an m.2 drive that was now getting around 3000 read and 2000 write speeds.
That made a HUGE difference, boot up was much faster, opening files/programs was much faster, even using the trackpad guessers seemed snappier.

My personal opinion is they crammed too many high powered components in a tiny ultrabook chassis.
Maybe after some Windows updates or something it will improve, but for now I wouldn't recommend.
It's not for gamers and it's not for someone who wants something ultra portable and doesn't care about gaming as the fans blare when you're just browsing the web.

title_x: One of the best laptops I've ever owned ... but, there are issues
text:
I'll be honest -- I'm torn. One part of me loves this laptop so much. I currently have six laptops and this is one of my favorites. However, there are some issue that just prevent it from being a five-star product. It's possible that I've just gotten a "lemon," but I feel I need to let you know about them. But first, the pros ...

WHAT I LOVE:
-THE LOOKS: This thing looks sharp. It's very sleek and, for the power it has inside, it's pretty thin. It's not an ultralight, but to have an RTX card and 11th Gen CPU, it's quite small.
-THE POWER: The Intel 11800h is pretty amazing. The RTX 3050 and the RAM, not as much. I have two other pretty powerful laptops: a Gigabyte Aorus with an RTX 2060 and a 10750h CPU and an Acer Nitro with an RTX 3050 and a 10300h CPU. In Geekbench CPU testing, the Worktop blows them away. It's 130% faster than both the Aorus and Nitro. However, when I ran an OpenCL test, the Nitro actually performed better -- albeit by less than 1% -- than the Worktop, which seemed odd. When I looked at the specs on Geekbench, it showed the RAM only running at 1600MHz on the Worktop, but running at 2933 on the Nitro. I thought that perhaps it was running in only single channel, so I went and checked the specs with CPU-Z and HWInfo and they both confirmed that the laptop is only running at 1600Mhz in dual channel. CPU-Z lists the native speed as 800Mhz, which seems odd for DDR4. However, Windows shows it at 3200Mhz. So, there you go: Three different places show three different speeds. I have no idea why a side-by-side comparison in Geekbench would show the Worktop's RAM running at half the speed, but that's what it shows, and I have heard that Geekbench would be more likely to show the actual RAM speed, which makes sense considering the CPU blows the other laptops away, but overall tests falter. However, I will say that the internal SSD is quite snappy and startup times are less than 15 seconds for me, not including logging into Windows.
-THE SCREEN: This is, hands down, the best laptop display I have ever owned. Even though it only has a 60Hz refresh rate, it blows away my Aorus laptop, which refreshes at 240Hz. The colors are spot-on, which is great for the work I do in desktop publishing, and 300 nits is plenty bright enough indoors and outdoors on overcast or party cloudy days. Watching video or looking at photos on this is a pure joy.
-AUDIO: I know it seems odd to hear that for a laptop, but there's something very pleasing about the sound of the built-in speakers. They're not going to win any bass competitions, obviously, but the mid and high end frequencies are very clear and crisp, especially the highs. It is necessary, however, to keep the volume slider above 50% almost all the time as the levels are just too low below that.
-THE BATTERY: Of all the laptops I currently -- or have ever -- owned, this has the best battery life, by far. I've been averaging about 9 hours on a charge, which is pretty amazing, considering I usually multitask quite often, going between remote desktop software, Photoshop and several Chrome tabs.

WHAT I DON'T LIKE:
-INTERNAL BLUETOOTH: I don't know why, but anytime I use a Bluetooth device with this laptop, it freezes constantly. I thought it might be a problem with Windows 10, so I made sure all of my laptops were updated to Windows 10 and tried my Bluetooth mice on all devices. This Worktop is the only one that has this problem. I searched so many YouTube videos trying to fix the problem, but I gave up. I had to use an external dongle for my wireless devices, and that works flawlessly.
-FusionTech ISSUES!: After using this for about a week or so, I closed the lid and put it in my backpack to take to a friend's house ... about a 10-minute trip. By the time I arrived, my laptop bag was burning hot. I opened it up and a huge heatwave struck me in the face. I went to grab the laptop, and it was so hot that I couldn't even touch it. For some reason, the FusionTech software decided to run some kind of troubleshooting program while it was in sleep mode, and it got so hot that it nearly overheated, throttling my CPU and turning my laptop's case into a hotplate.
-BLOATWARE: There's way too much FusionTech software that comes with this. If you look in the FusionTech folder, there are tons of applications that seem unnecessary. There's also a preinstalled version of McAfee that behaves more like malware than an anti-virus program. I uninstalled it immediately. It even attaches itself to all of your web browsers without asking. Bad move, FusionTech.
-ERGONOMICS: The keyboard itself is fine and pretty easy to type on. The key travel is incredibly small, so if you're used to a mechanical keyboard, you probably won't like this. However, I do love the addition of the numpad as I need it for shortcuts in the software I use at work. My main issue with the design, however, is that my wrist constantly brushes against the touchpad, which causes my cursor to jump around and places it in odd positions while I type. Also, the fingerprint sensor is in an odd position at the top right. My Acer laptops have the sensor in the corner of the touchpad, which makes more sense, IMO.
-BATTERY DRAIN: I'm not sure what happened, but one night while using it, the battery drained from 100% to 0 overnight. When I went to check Windows to see what happened, it showed no applications running. I have no idea what happened. Maybe it was a Windows issue, but it's worth mentioning as it's never happened on my other laptops.

CONCLUSION:
I struggled on a star rating. I went back and forth between 4 and 5 stars so many times, it's not funny. Ultimately, I'm giving it 4 stars to allow some room for growth. I will continue to use this laptop and will see if these odd issues with battery drain, Bluetooth and overheating persist. If they seem like random anomalies or problems with Windows 10 itself, I will return and upgrade my review to 5 stars. For now, though, it's just a "great laptop." It's so close to being an "excellent laptop," but for me, it's just not there.

title_x: 300 hz Screen and RTX 3070 Lives up to the hype - CPU runs hot
text:
I went from a very budget friendly gamin pc laptop to this Advance M15 R4. I opted for the 300mhz screen and RTX 3070 GPU that runs on the Intel Core i7-10870H and 16gb RAM, to be clear which one I am reviewing.
Now just because I had a budget laptop previously does not mean I haven't had my share of beefy systems in the past years as I am a veteran gamer. So my reaction comes with experience.

Build Quality
The look, the feel, the presentation and build quality are top notch. The laptop feels solid. Its WAY lighter than my last laptop. Its not Macbook level but for a gaming laptop Im surprised at how sleek and shallow it is. I work as a graphic designer so showing up to a client meeting with a big ole ugly gaming computer was just out of the question for me. If your client isn't a gamer, they wont think anything of your laptop other than that glowing alien head looks cool as heck! The RGB lighting is subtle but looks amazing. Very well designed and it can be fully customized or even turned off if you so desire. The lighting across the keys is not 100% consistent however. Its like they put just enough to light it up but there are some areas that vary in brightness. Its subtle and definitely not a deal breaker. I also notice that when set to white (which is what I like to set it at during the day) is not quite white but a little pink. So I manually added in a bit of blue to it so it looks better.

Its unfortunate other reviews have received damaged goods. But that should be on a seller review not the product review. Please keep that in mind.

Performance
Ill start with the 300hz monitor. All I can say is wow. Nice and bright. Clear enough. Its not 2k/4k but its clean. Not sure you would want a 4k laptop monitor (yet) but maybe in a few years. The refresh rate for gaming is just awesome. Seeing FPS go into the 200s on some games is just butter. Love the screen.

3070 GPU - For me this GPU hit the sweet spot for me. Its not so overpriced as the 3080 or 3090 (or hard to find) so I can keep several hundred dollars off the cost but its not going to be outdated in a year or 2 which I feel like the 3060 is close to that already. For whatever its worth, this GPU handles most AAA games that Ive thrown at it. Everything renders amazingly and smooth as silk. And when I am doing my graphic work, video editing, or even some 3D modeling, it doesn't miss a beat.

AND I can also say the GPU does great in this machine with heat. Very rarely am I pushing it to its max. And even tho the Advance software allows me to overclock the GPU, I have left it in standard mode and its done phenomenal.

Which brings us to the Intel Core i7-10870H CPU. Its a great CPU, multi-thread, latest design, runs great. It can handle the games and even more so, it can handle my motion graphic and 3d modeling work easily. However it runs really HOT in this chassis. So much so that I often max it out at 100C. Good thing I monitor it closely and sometimes just have to take a break after playing a AAA game for a bit. I do notice if I have both the GPU and CPU fans going it does a better job at cooling down, but its unfortunate because then the fan noise gets loud. They are not obnoxious fans by any means, but still, a fan is a fan and it would be nice to not have to worry ALL the time. Im sure this is also a byproduct of how slim the laptop is so, if I had to choose, Ill take the slimmer design any day. Just need to find a good cooling pad that works.

Now for the big bummer...
RAM is fixed and cannot be changed. While I am generally getting 2999mhz out of RMA, as someone who likes to tinker this was a hard one to decide upon. Mostly because it comes back to the gaming laptops that do allow you to tinker are often big and bulky and was not what I wanted for this round. I understand why companies make this choice, doesn't mean I have to like it, but for something that cannot be changed out, at least its high quality and is running at a high rate with no issues. Keep this in mind, as I think this comes down to personal choice. Id rather have high quality components I cant change rather than giving the company an excuse to put crappy unusable components simply because you CAN change them out, which is usually the story with other gaming laptops that do allow you to change out the ram. Just my 2 cents. So if you are deciding to get one of these, be sure to go for 16gb or more. 8gb just isnt going to cut it for very long.

On the upside, it does have 3 bays for SSDs. x2 2280 slots and x1 2242(I believe, which is the shorter version). It comes with the the first 2280 slot occupied but all are NVMe so that is great. I saw some reports online to NOT get the RAID setup as it is wildly under-performing so just go with a straight 1tb and then add the additional space you need. I opted for another 1tb which is working out. If you like to download a LOT of games, then add a 2tb to be safe.

Battery life is non-existent. You may get 2 hrs at the very BEST if you turn everything down, but never more than that. My last laptop was no different. I have not read one review on any powerhouse gaming laptop that has great battery life though, so, if you plan on gaming you need to be plugged in anyway. Not to mention, the GPU wont get the full load it needs on battery. Most laptops are like this as well so to me, not really a point I used to decide upon. They all suck and to run games you still need to be plugged in so if you are looking for a laptop to carry around campus or on the road, you shouldn't even be considering a gaming laptop anyway. :D

Overall I am very happy with the purchase. If you are a tinkerer, and want what you want, then you may have to look somewhere else. Mostly good. I've had this laptop since May 2021. When I first got it out of the box, I called FusionTech, and a tech there set the whole thing up remotely for me. I took him about an hour, but it might have taken me forever by myself. It's all good, except -- (and none of these are deal breakers in my opinion):

1) The laptop tends to run hot. I have a VR headset and when the laptop is connected to that, either with a cable or wirelessly, the laptop gets really hot, especially the keyboard, and the fans run like crazy. Of course, I'm not using the keyboard when I'm using the VR headset. I called FusionTech and the lady said it will be OK, and I posted to a VR headset FB page, and the advice there was not to adjust the settings, and that it will be OK -- but it gets really hot -- almost immediately upon cranking up the VR connection. I never use the VR with the laptop for over 1/2 hour at a time because I'm concerned, even though I've been told it will be OK. I'm new to VR and gaming laptops, and maybe computers are with VR just are hot and their fans run like crazy. I'm always very careful to make sure air can get underneath the laptop.

2) The charger cord has a HUGE heavy charger box associated with it. I guess that's for surge protection. My main problem with it isn't the size or weight. It is that the cord doesn't stay plugged into the charger box thing. The slightest jiggling seems to dislodge it enough that the little blue light on the cord goes off. The battery life doesn't seem to be anything spectacular, so I don't like it that it can be so easily unintentionally unplugged. I'm thinking about putting something on it to keep it plugged in.

3) The housing of the laptop has a bit of a cheap feel. When opening the lid/screen, the hinge creaks a little.

I got the Nvidia GForce RTX2060 graphics card and 16GB Ram. I thought that the price was good for the features. So far, despite the comments above, I'm not regretting the purchase.

title_x: FusionTech at their best...  They hit this one outta the park..
text:
This my be the best laptop in the FusionTech range.. I have had a Macbook Air M1 since December and a FusionTech ABC 13 (1185G7 processor) since April.. Both are great laptops and compete directly with each other. This new laptop makes a few design decisions that while make it for a slightly thicker notebook make for a more versatile laptop than a no compromise ultralight such the ABC 13 or Macbook Air. As nice as and as big of improvement over previous Intel onboard graphics the Iris XE is no match for the Geforce MX450 in Worktop 13. You get a 2k screen which is a match for Apple's retina and a better option than FusionTechs ABC which either use the battery draining 4k screen or a FHD+ plus screen. It also has ncie matte finish with better brightness than my ABC.

The processor I7-11370H in real world benchmarks is roughly 10% faster than 1185G7 in ABC. In addition while only having a slightly larger battery it seems to last about a third longer. I have not had any issues with heat on the Worktop 13 BTW..

Footprint wise the I-13 is about the same as the macbook air and about 1/4" thicker. The bezelless ABC is about a 1/2" shorter and narrower. On the other had the extra space is utilized well including a real USB-A port, HDMI and two thunderbolt ports. In a addition it has a very clever hinge design the lifts the back of the of the keyboard and improves ergonomics.. The case is all metal, which seems to not attract fingerprints (which ABC's carbon fiber wrist rest is pretty bad about.)

If you have read this far you garnered I like this laptop... I will be selling my ABC which despite the criticism in comparison to this model is still one of the best laptops on the market. In my case I'm willing to have a slightly larger laptop in exchange for not carry a dock or dongles and getting a bump in battery life. The best aspect of this laptop is it's value proposition it is about 400 bucks less than an equivalent ABC 13.. Highly recommended.

title_x: A waste of specs and money
text:
When I first read the specs for the 5310 I was really intrigued. It sounded like a whole lot of machine in a very small package. But it doesn't take long to realize that the 5310 crams in a lot of unnecessary hardware and cost for virtually no improved performance.

CPU

The Intel Core i7-11370H. The idea behind this chip was to compete with Ryzen in the laptop/ultra portable gaming sector of the market. But after their previous 6 and 8 core 10 generation series the 11370H is a step back for Intel having only 4 cores, which for 2021 just isn't enough anymore.

The 11370H might shine in single threaded productivity tasks but that's where the pros of the chip end. Paired with a high end GPU (like in the Asus TUF Dash F15 which sports a 3070) the 11370H is passable in modern titles that aren't CPU bound, thought the performance is well behinds competitors. Unfortunately the Worktop 5310's GPU is far from high end.

GPU

NVIDIA claims the GeForce MX450 slots somewhere in between a 1050 and a 1650. Frankly I don't know enough to be able to compare the three GPUs but my experience with the MX450 is I need to know to come to a conclusion here. For the most part, modern games are unplayable. Anything with higher-end graphics is a no go, you will have to drop your resolution down to 1280x720 to eek above 30-40 fps. At low settings, 1080p the best I could get from Rise of the Tomb Raider was a "steady" 20 fps. On medium settings I was getting ~30 fps on Firewatch. When it comes to gaming on the 5310 I'd say your best best is pixelated/low poly games or legacy system emulation.

PRODUCTIVITY/PERFOMANCE

Even here I wouldn't hold out high expectations for the 5310. Any sort of multi-tasking bogs down the CPU. After two weeks I've yet to have WebEx run successfully for more than two minutes before it hangs and then crashes. Web browsing is smooth, and it's only here I can appreciate the mostly unnecessary headroom offered by the 16gb of ram because I do love my multiple tabs.

Media consumption is another confusing aspect of the 5310. At times the display can be sharp and beautiful, but comparatively speaking even at max brightness it's a little dim. And the native resolution of 2560x1600, while good for some tasks, feels awkward and an odd choice. While it's not exactly rare the 16:10 aspect ratio is a lot less common than 16:9 so expect to frequently see black bars in any gaming or media. And although I appreciate the sharpness of the QHD resolution I wonder why FusionTech chose to pair this resolution with a CPU geared towards 1080p performance?

CONCLUSION

Design wise this is a sleek little ultra-portable laptop. It's lightweight, minimalist, and a pleasure to work on with the few tasks it handles well. Unfortunately it feels like FusionTech shoved in a bunch of unnecessary, expensive, and poorly paired hardware to create this mostly unusable, mismatched Frankenstein of a machine. And on top of all that the various FusionTech bloatware included makes this even more undesirable.

title_x: May be I expected too much!
text:
When I first saw the spec of this FusionTech laptop, I was thinking this one has all the things I find lacking in current HP HP Pavilion 15z. Thinks such like a slightly larger and better display screen @3K and support HDR, Thunderbolt 4 connection, a discrete video card for better 3D, even I am not a gamer. The tradeoffs are the display is not a touch screen, no mention of the keyboard is backlit (turn out it is) or not and Win 10 Home (it has since been corrected).

When I receive the unit, the first thing to feel is its weight. The packaging only contain the laptop, the AC adapter and a piece of disclosures, no other accessories nor manual. Although everything are online these days, something like keyboard functions that are unique to the laptop is still better to have a printed chart.

Even with a larger screen (16" vs 15.6"), this laptop is barely larger than the HP. Its weights however about half lb. heavier (about 4.4 lb vs 3.8 lb). While half lb may not sound much, it does made this laptop feels less portable.

Turning on this laptop I was surprised to find two things, the first is it came with Win 10 Pro instead of Win 10 Home. The original Amazon had the Win 10 Home in the title but Win 10 Pro in the description. It is good that it does came with Win 10 Pro. I think for the BitLocker encryption function alone, no laptop should ship with Win 10 Home anymore.

The second surprise was the keyboard is actually backlighted however, it is so dime that, even at brightest setting, it is still way too dim and it is actually worse than just paint white on black under low light condition. The keyboard are full size with numeric key pad and a large touch pad. The power button is at upper right and doubles as finger print reader. The keys while not the worst I have had on laptop, it has more of the rubbery feel than the HP.

I had high hope on the display as my desktop PC's monitor is HDR capable and I find the HP laptop's display wanting. I was very disappointed to find this FusionTech laptop's HDR is ONLY for video streaming, regular HDR and WCG apps are not supported, at lest not at default settings and I have not find way to get them on. As shown on the photo, side by side with the HP, one hardly notice much difference and the HP has much brighter backlighted keyboard.

As for performance, I was shocked to find the HP has higher Passmark Performance 10.1 than this FusionTech as the HP is AMD Ryzen 7 4700 based, although very capable should not have higher performance than this one as it does not have discrete video card and the CPU is a generation older. Upon looking at induvial scores, it seems this laptop only has significant lower 2D video and slightly lower memory score. This unit has significant higher CPU and 3D video scores as expected. On UserBenchmark, this one did get higher rating It seems it is Passmark's rating at fault. However, I was very disappointed to see such low score on 2D display as photo editing is important to me. More important than games in fact.

This laptop does not have an Ethernet port. Only WiFi. It uses Intel AX201 card that only support Intel chipset vs the Intel AX200 used by the HP. One would think Intel with Intel will give AX201 an edge, alas it is not so. Side by side on the same spot, using my desktop PC as test server with wired 2.5GbE to the WiFi 6E router (used as AP) testing 5GHz band with WPA3 security, this laptop's WiFi is sub par not only to the HP's AX200, it is also worse than my smartphone. Luckily if you are using this more like a desktop replacement than actual laptop, you can get an Ethernet to USB adapter that I have tested on the Thunderbolt 4 port to get 2.5Gbps no problem.

Speaking of Thunderbolt 4 port, while I don't have any devices to test it at 40Gbps, I did test it at 10Gbps without problem. The PD charging however, while a nice feature point on the spec, it has less practical use. The reason is this laptop is power hungry. The AC adapter came with it is 130W vs HP's 65W. I have not seen such high wattage AC adapter for years. While it is understandable the 3050 graphics chip is heavy power user, this made even 65W PD charger not able to keep up the usage and thus only able to charge while the laptop is not in use or switch to the IGP.

Speaking of high power usage, this one also generates a lot of the heat an fan noise when the 3050 is in use. the vents at back bottom can easily reach over 50 deg C. That also made this more of desktop replacement than something on your lap.

The NVME SSD that came with this laptop is quite good. Using Crystal DiskMark, it is on par with top PCIE3 NVMEs. While 16B RAM is more than enough for most people, for photo editing that keep several memory hog program running at same time, 32GB would have been better. Luckily, it is not difficult to upgrade the RAM.

This is one of the more service or upgrade friendly laptop on the market, all you need to do is unscrew the visible screws on the back. No hidden screws under rubber foot or label.

The first thing to note and not to my liking is the hinge design. I had more so many laptop got broken hinge broken with this type of design before made me fear this one would not last either.

There are TWO NVME slots in this laptop, however, one is limited to 2230 size, while the other can hold up to 2280 size. As one can see from the internal layout, it should not be that difficult to accommodate both for 2280 size, as the 2280 size NVMEs are more readily available and at lower per TB price. It is too bad the engineers decided to go with easy route. The good thing is heatsink are provided for both. A further good thing is the NVME came with the unit is 2230 in size. Although it was installed on the 2280 slot with adapter, it is easy to move it to the 2230 slot. This is important because the 2280 slow is PCIE4 ready vs the 2230 size is only PCIE3. I have test Samsung 980 Pro, a PCIE4 NVME on the 2280 slot and the speed while slightly lower than my desktop, it is excellent for the laptop.

Changing the memory is easy as the memory slots are next the NVMEs under the flaps.

I don't know if I can swap the AX201 WiFi card with AX210 as the HP would not and the current AX210 driver has WiFi6E WPA3 compatibility problem, so I probably will wait a little but that AX201's poor performance is a let down.

Now I like to talk about system recovery that I hope you never need to do as this FusionTech's system recovery was another down side of the laptop most people would not encounter. I normally not just back up but clone my working system NVME so that I have instant recovery. For this one because it is new, I only have the benchmark programs installed and I was trying to test out dual boot, bad idea. While the FusionTech BIOS is much better than HP, it only sees one Win boot manger instead of two (one for each NVME), on my desktop I can easily select which one to boot in the BIOS and not so in this laptop and to make it worse, after a few failed attempt, the boot manger on the original boot manager was ruined. First, I tried the FusionTech OS recovery assistant, no go. After a few unsuccessful trials, even the usual Win reset option is no long available.

I then tried using FusionTech's USB recovery imaging program, to download it from FusionTech's web site, you need the service tag of the laptop. If the tag does not match, the during boot, it will stop. This is nonsense logic, they can just check to see if it is FusionTech product, demanding exact service tag is not necessary and aggravate already bad situation worse. The FusionTech's web site's insurrections is also out of date or at least did not match my
BIOS. For example, there is NO legacy boot option on my BIOS.

To make dad thing even worse, the USB recovery program says HDD not found! Even when the BIOS has no difficulties to find both NVME and the USB. Makes one wonder whether FusionTech has fully test the recovery program or not.

Just when I was ready to gave up on FusionTech's recovery, I tried a last ditch boot and surprise, the Win reset option came back which was linked to FusionTech's own reset option and after several hours I finally got the laptop back to "new" condition. This recovery experience left me a rather low opinion on FusionTech's recovery utilities. If taking the recovery experience into consideration, I would only give this laptop a 3 stars instead of 4.

Overall, if you are looking for a decent laptop as desktop replacement with a decent size screen, playing some not too demanding games, this one is an ok option but probably not the best overall option.

title_x: You get used to the fans... mostly
text:
This is a very good little general-use laptop. As a gaming machine, it's so-so, but outside of dedicated gaming laptops that cost much more, that's relatively good.

This machine gets warm during casual use, and it will get hot if you push it with anything approaching a demanding game. The fans are going to run most of the time.

As for gaming performance, it can handle modern stuff, as long as you turn the setting down. This is in no way a replacement for a recent gaming desktop PC, but you can game with it. You may want to invest in a laptop cooling pad with built-in fans if you're going to use it in demanding applications.

Other than that, the build quality seems good. There's no "flex" and the hinge design seems good. The hinge lifts the body away from the table, which is a hint - this little machine craves airflow.

Performance on non-gaming tasks is good. The keyboard and trackpad both feel good. The webcam is nothing impressive, similar to what you'd get on a low-end laptop. The physical shutter is a nice touch, but I had a little trouble using it on mine. It's pretty stiff.

title_x: Beautiful Screen and Perfect for the creator on the go
text:
Was able to get this laptop through the vine program for my wife who is a full time photographer, who uses photoshop cc and Lightroom daily. This powers through editing and with the 4K touch screen, they not only look amazing, the pixel density is ideal for zooming in. She wanted something sleek, powerful, can edit hi res pics and video, can play games if wanted. This hit all those boxes! If you need a powerful machine with a beautiful screen, this is a great choice.

Pros
- Fantastic Screen! Might be the most beautiful screen I’ve seen on a laptop, for me it even tops the retina in MacBooks.
- powerful processor. The 8core 16thread cpu are more than enough to power through programs like butter. For the price I wish it had an i9.
- Ram- 16gb at 3200mhz, it is plenty but this price it could have at least been 32gb.
- Battery last decently. My wife gets 5ish hours sitting on the couch editing at full brightness.
- looks fantastic! Has a Mac book esque quality to it. Very sleek.

Cons - the reason for 4 instead of five stars
- The lack of usb a 3.0 ports is sad, should have 1 on board. The huge hub it comes with only has 1. Would much rather have 2 thunder and 2 3.0.
- The gpu should’ve at least been a 3060. With a 3050, i7 and 16gb of ram nothing is top end. I have an Advance the same price with an i7, but it also had 32gb of ram and an rtx 3080, 2 high end specs. To me the 4K screen doesn’t justify all 3 to be mid range.

If this was $2000 or had 2 more upgrades (ram, cpu or gpu) it would be more worth of the $2600 price tag. But if you need a phenomenal screen and the ability to create and lightly game, a solid choice.

text: This is a decent laptop, once it’s upgraded. Out of the box, with 8GB RAM, and a 1TB HDD, it is molasses slow. Loading Windows took over 5 minutes, easy. And trying to play a game like Rust? FusionTech loads these things FULL of bloated software, so your first order of business is to delete all of it. Then upgrade the RAM, and get an SSD. These have a slot for NVME m.2 SSD. I bumped my RAM to 16GB, and got a 500gig m.2 SSD, and WHAT A DIFFERENCE! Windows boots up to the desktop within 8 seconds. Rust loads within a minute or two. The entire computer is transformed from sluggish to super snappy and responsive. The specs are decent, but it really really needs an SSD to shine.

text: I ended up going with the M15 R4 RTX 3070. On paper the specs are very impressive, but at the end of the day, it only matters if the equipment is capable of utilizing these specs. If you're going to run AAA title games, your laptop is going to overheat and shut down unless you know how to undervolt it. It's pretty pitiful that you have handicap your laptop to run it, especially when factoring the price. It's absolutely lazy engineering by Advance. Even the most modest games will push the thermals north of 80 Celsius. Games like Back 4 Blood and Cyperpunk register consistently at 100 Celsius (which is the maximum temperature the laptop can safely run without damaging the hardware) until the laptop has a heat stroke and then dies. I bought a cooling pad just so that I can rest the laptop on my lap without singeing my poor pubes. There are videos online that'll teach you how to undervolt the laptop. I personally prefer ThrottleStop, but it's pathetic that I have to utilize it just to play the games that this laptop was supposedly built to play. Please read up on this issue on Reddit before you commit. This is a known issue with this laptop. I wish I had done some more research before purchasing this furnace in laptop's clothing.

text:
Update: Not sure what happened to my previous review for this. TLDR, I had the infamous trackpad wobble. I managed to get it replaced by FusionTech; the warranty service was a bit frustrating at the start but they did get me depot repair w/ Fedex Overnight boxes. I don't like how at this price point you're going for the trackpad lottery, although this is an excellent-looking design with good performance despite the weight.

As a disclaimer before, I did get this unit from Vine. I am not sponsored by FusionTech nor Amazon in any sort of way, I just one day went on Vine after meeting at work and found this available for review. This review is also really lengthy so read at your own risk.

Short version:

I got the infamous trackpad wobble after a few hours. FusionTech your QC sucks, your customers are paying this much money and you can’t even get the trackpad right. Apart from that, this is one of the most stylish and capable Windows laptops out there.

Performance is definitely a worthy update from the 2020 models, the 3050 model is fine and apparently the 3060 model no longer has battery drain issues while on the charger. It’s pricey with a good design, but FusionTech’s quality control, especially with the trackpad design, holds this thing back as much as the butterfly keyboard on MacBooks .

If you use the expresscharge setting it goes from 10%-80% in 50 minutes on idle/web browsing. Battery life is decent

The keyboard is good. I wouldn’t say it’s as good as a Thinkpad, the key travel is comparable to a standard Thinkpad keyboard but with more actuation force, or a longer, stiffer Magic Keyboard. The display is excellent

If price is not an issue, and you want one of the best-looking windows laptops, and you need great CPU performance and not too much GPU performance or casually game, or you need one of the largest displays you can get on a laptop in this form factor with performance to back it up, this is a good option. However if you need more performance and don’t care about the form factor, some gaming laptops are 60% of the price. If you only need a large display and don’t care about the performance just go for the LG Gram 17 to also get a massive battery and weight savings. If you need reliability, I mean Thinkpads have one of the best included warranties if something does go wrong, and the latest X1 Extreme/P1 has a 16in display while being lighter than the 15in ABC 9510. There’s also waiting until the latest Macbook Pros with Apple Silicon to come out, which will probably cost approximately the same, should offer similar performance, and should have better battery life.

Long version:

With that out of the way, let’s get started to how this is actually my “2nd unit”. So one thing that plagues the ABC 17 (and the newer ABC 15 when they switched to all type-C) is the trackpad. Both of my units had problems. The first one I received had thermal issues as well (where the CPU package would thermal-throttle prematurely, more on this later) and left side of the trackpad behaved differently than the right. So I returned and requested another unit, and guess what, the left side of the trackpad has a tiny rattle when pressed down… Both of these happened within a few hours of opening, so yeah. I understand how nicer a bigger trackpad seems on paper and on looks, but as someone with a Macbook Pro 16 for a work laptop, a large trackpad doesn’t mean a good thing, and it’s even worse for an ABC. Oh also 2 finger operation is a bit bad, where sometimes your clicks don’t register. This I feel like is something that you shouldn’t have to deal with when you’re paying this much for a laptop, hence my main criticism of this device. Come on FusionTech, keep your act together for once that’s not about selling warranties…

About that point btw, I did kind of “fix it” myself. If you search up FusionTech ABC 17 trackpad wobble, there’s a video about fixing the trackpad for the 15in 9500 from Mash IT. He added some tape to the chassis to basically pad against the battery. For the 17in there’s foam surrounding it, so instead I put a layer of electrical tape on the back of the battery, where there’s an indent where the trackpad metal clips sinks into. Don’t block that part up, but on the battery put a layer of tape. I mostly fixed it with 1 layer, 2 layer was too stiff, but you might want to put 2 layers instead of 1 on the caps-lock side of the trackpad. I ended up taking it apart and putting 2 layers on the caps-lock side and so far the wobble seems to be gone. If your right side wobbles you might want to place the extra layer on the backspace-side of the battery. You may still end up with residual rattle, but it’s much less than before.

Beyond the critical failure on FusionTech for their quality control on the trackpads, let’s first talk about its appearance. This has to be one of the most gorgeous looking laptops. The bezels are very thin, typical of the ABC line. The keyboard looks great and as someone who doesn’t like numpads I’m perfectly fine with the layout. The display can be opened with one hand. I use a skin because I’m actually not a fan of aluminum, but the quality is very much there, unlike the trackpad.

Now the keyboard. Like I said before, I’m fine with no numpad, because it doesn’t offset my hands on the left/right. Palm rejection on the trackpad is actually okay, but because it’s so big sometimes using it with 2 fingers can cause the palm rejection to trigger because another part of your hand is resting on the trackpad. The keys are decent, but then again I swear by Thinkpads, so I would give it a feel of a stiffer Thinkpad keyboard. The travel feels more similar to the Magic Keyboard or the X1 Nano (which has a reduced travel compared to the rest of the Thinkpad lineup), but because of that stiffness I does feel better than the X1 Nano because the keys don’t bottom out faster, but that stiffness feels tiring because I feel I need to apply extra force on the keys. Compared to the Macbook Pro 16 it is “quieter” because the keys have less of a “clack” sound to them. Brightness is now on F6 and F7 instead of arrow-up and down, which means I can reach the display brightness adjustment on a FusionTech laptop with one hand. Something I found weird, it’s either the size of the laptop or the unusually large trackpad, but I’ve found myself to tilt my hand a lot more compared to typing on usual laptops, even on my Macbook Pro 16 work laptop, maybe it’s just instinct from typical Windows trackpad palm rejection problems, or I’m used to smaller laptops, but I do seem to have more typos, not because of the keys, but this weird quirk. No fault of the laptop I would say, just an observation.

A lot of people say the ABC 17 is the best speakers pretty much in its class on the Windows side, well I fired up Gregoire Blanc’s Clair de Lune and Uamee’s Il-76 on both the ABC and my Macbook Pro 16 work laptop. It was no contest, the Macbook blows the ABC out of the water. Sure, the sound is okay, but as soon as you go over 40% volume you can really feel that the speakers are straining and becoming more grainy, where as the Macbook had no problems. I mean sure, it’s one of the best sounding Windows laptop I’ve heard, but going from Il-76 on the Macbook to the ABC sounded like a muddy mess, the ABC just can’t keep up on the speaker department. If I want to be Dankpods about it I guess the ABC prioritizes on the higher-end instead of having a heavier bass, but these are laptop speakers, most of the time you want volume and bass in the first place…

The display is just awesome with a bit of an asterisk. Sure it’s a lot of extra money for the 4k touch, which isn’t even that useful for most people and is kind of there to just hog battery life (FusionTech rates max power consumption for the 1200p at 5.06W, and the 4k at 13.73W, to give you an idea). Touch is nice, it is bright and colors are very vibrant, so it’s really just if you want to get it because you want “4k”. The response isn’t that great though so don’t expect it to be really good for gaming. Why I say an asterisk is because it can look overly saturated, and the reflective display can look not so uniform when auto-brightness kicks in.

On the topic of the display though I do need to bring something that I had major complaints about back when I had a 2018 Macbook Pro 13. The display cable. If you look at the vents in the back, you can see the very large, exposed display cable that stretches across that gap, very similar to the Type-C Macbook Pros have their display. I had the 2018 which was “Free” from flexgate, aka stagelight, but I was shooketh back then at the thought of Apple putting exposed display cables. Well FusionTech managed to outdo Apple this time. Unlike Apple however, you can very easily grab the laptop by that gap in the back when it’s folded, and possibly touch and damage the display cable. I don’t think this is an issue observed by the ABC 17 from the previous year’s model, but having that thought is a bit unnerving.

The camera is fine. I don’t care about webcam quality as much, but it is just 720p and there are better options out there. Windows Hello IR is a nice touch, although this is one of those IR cameras that have both the IR combined with the normal camera, so you can’t just cover the normal camera and still get facial recognition. I also wished it had a shutter like almost every Lenovo laptop nowadays, although I can understand how difficult that might be with how little the bezels are. One thing I do have to mention, is something I’ve seen on Macbook Pros since 2008, but only twice on Windows, specifically the X1 Carbon 2nd gen (yes the touchbar one), and the X380 Yoga: an ambient light sensor. There’s not that many windows laptops out there with this sensor for automatic brighrness adjustment that Macbooks pretty much had for over 10 years now. The ABC 17 has it, and although sometimes it can be a bit choppy, it’s still a nice feature that may be a gimmick, but I’m a sucker for gimmicks and as a Mac user I will take every opportunity to strike back at Apple.

I/O is tricky. FusionTech basically went ABC 15 2-in-1 (the 9575) on their newer ABC 15 and 17. My friend who has a 2017 ABC 15 doesn’t want to upgrade because of the lack of type-A ports (and the smaller battery too for the 15in). I used a Macbook Pro 13 from 2019 so I made the type-C transition, so type-C ports isn’t really a problem for me. If it is though, the older ABC still has type-A, the LG gram is still an option if you don’t need too much performance, or go for anything Thinkpad that isn’t the X1 Nano. There is a full-size SD card, it doesn’t fit flush but it’s better than not having any. Speeds maxed out at 100mbps for my Lexar 1066x, and I swear there’s no card reader that maxes out its “advertised max read” of 160mbps so I’ll blame the card since the card reader is supposed to do better than that. At least they didn’t remove the headphone jack.

I did end up upgrading the RAM and storage, to 32GB of Gskill 3200mhz ram, and adding in a Crucial P5 1TB. It does take a bit of work taking this apart. You need a pretty sharp, plastic spudger, and then slide it along the edges to “pop” or “prop” the bottom chassis out (FusionTech has a guide on it). After that, just pull up on the battery to disconnect power (or not if your name is Linus Sebastian). You do need to remove the battery screw to remove the heat spreader for the SSD. They didn’t put a plastic layer for mine on the empty slot so it’s kind of just drop-in, then putting the heat spreader back on. I don’t have a PCIE gen-4 SSD, so I couldn’t test compatibility, but technically it should be compatible according to FusionTech.

Since we are on disassembly I should talk about repasting. I didn’t do it, because I know someone who also bought this, repasted it, and got WAYYY worse results on CPU. Apparently (and this is backed up by someone on reddit), the area of the heatsink that makes contact with the CPU is very “rough”, and repasting may not be able to get into the small imperfections that are there on the heatsink. This is kind of confirmed by my friend who recovered back to 97% of his pre-repaste performance by using a thinner paste like Arctic MX4 instead of Noctua NT-H1. Apparently he did get 5C cooler on the RTX 3050, but for me I’m just not going to repaste until a few years down the line, assuming this thing makes it that far :/ Oh also I’ve taken it apart 5 times and the clips at the front for the bottom panel are already wearing out. Thankfully the bottom are held by the screws, magnets, and the design is much better than the ABC 15 9575 (the 15in 2-in-1) where one side of the laptop is held by clips, where if those clips break, you need to replace the keyboard assembly.

Now for performance and thermals. For CPU, I went with Cinebench R20 which it scored over 4800. It’s pretty good, but it also did that at a peak boost power consumption of a whopping 116W. And I thought a 4800/5800H doing 80W was extreme (I come from either desktops, where power consumption matters less than temps, or ultrabooks, where boosting to 45W for 2 seconds is like...a really high number). Of course it doesn’t stay boosted like that forever, it settles down to more ~90ishW, which still feels like a lot to me. Thermals at that time was 91C on the CPU and 100C on the CPU package, so it was very much redlining itself. The vapor chamber cooling I think is doing its work, as this kind of power consumption and temps would probably not be possible on any mere mortal heatsink design. You can’t undervolt because Tiger Lake doesn’t support SGX, and even if it did it probably would’ve been locked because of the Plundervolt vulnerability. As for the GPU, it was 70C while running Unigine Heaven and scored a 3036.

Most reviews out there have the 3060 unit, which is very capable. The 3050 however as expected, not that much. I mean sure, at fullscreen 1200p Minecraft w/ optifine it will hit over 270fps and ~110fps in Payday 2, it’s probably better than the 1650ti. It should also support DLSS which is good. Just don’t expect it to be revolutionary compared to something like a 1660ti. If you curb your enthusiasm and compare it to the older 1650 or the 1650ti, you should be okay.

The stock RAM is the Samsung m471a1g44ab0-cwe, which use the worse 16gb chips. This isn’t surprising even if it wasn’t a FusionTech, since the industry seems to be saving a few bucks on larger-capacity chips at the cost of bandwidth. I don’t remember the exact difference, but

The stock SSD is the Micron 2300. It seems to be an OEM version of the Crucial P5, since they both use the exact same controller. At least this isn’t something FusionTech cheaped out on, but that doesn’t deserve anything special since computers of this class should have this type of SSD performance. Performance is typical of a good gen 3 NVME SSD. One thing to note is like usual, FusionTech sets drives to RAID mode in the bios, so if you switch it back to AHCI, you will get the typical blue screen about device not found. It happened to me, I couldn’t fix it, realized that the bloatware was not worth going through anyways, and just did a clean reinstall on the 1TB Crucial P5 I added in. Do be warned, FusionTech hardware seems to be EXTREMELY driver dependent, to the point after a new windows install the touchscreen didn’t even work. Windows updates did solve all those problems, so don’t be afraid if things act up after a clean install.

I used the stock drive, and then did a clean-reinstall. FusionTech includes incredible amounts of bloatware in the stock install. It’s not as annoying as other FusionTech apps that I’ve seen, but it does get pretty annoying. The only 2 you really need are the FusionTech Update and Power Manager. The Power Manager gives you some bios power settings (like battery charge behavior) and performance (optimized, quiet, performance, etc) in Windows instead of going to the bios. I would’ve liked the power manager if it had a taskbar feature like Lenovo Vantage where I can change power options on-the-fly, instead of spending a “pretty long time” to launch the app.

Linux support can be described in 1 word: yesn’t. Sure there’s plenty of info and solutions out there, there’s even a driver for the fingerprint sensor, but you have a lot of hoops to jump through, especially on Ubuntu 21.04 (I use PopOS); the speakers doesn’t even work out of the box on Linux, just be prepared to go through the typical cycle of configuration. This isn’t an old Thinkpad with god-tier driver support.

Charging speed was 50 minutes from 10% to 80% on the express-charge setting while idling and web browsing, so the charger can cram a lot of power to the battery (it went to 100% after 1 hour and 46 minutes btw). I’m not sure how healthy this is for the battery, and I normally use the custom threshold 50%-80% (because I use it on a desk a lot), even though charging speed on that setting is much slower.

The ultimate problem with this is both the unreliable trackpad quality, and the price. As a long-time Thinkpad user I tend to look at equivalent Thinkpad options, and the new 4th gen X1 Extreme got upgraded to a 16in display, at a weight 0.5lbs lighter than the ABC15, and even has up to the RTX 3070. The base model is 1600p instead of 1200p for the display w/ a 3050ti instead of 3050, at a price (At the time of writing this review) of <$2000. The stock 1-year warranty for Thinkpads based on my experience, compared to my friend’s experience with a 3-year FusionTech warranty, is much better in terms of getting service if something breaks. It doesn’t matter for the ABC 17 to have a massive trackpad if the design is as flawed as the butterfly keyboard.

So overall, as much as I want to like this device, having to deal with a defective trackpad and trackpad design makes it really unsavory. At this amount of money I’m honestly going to say just spend the extra and get the 3060 model, you’re already paying this much. There are plenty of options out there that are cheaper with more performance. The Gigabyte Aero comes with the same CPU w/ a RTX 3060 as low as $1350. The HP Omen w/ the R5 5600H and the 3060 can go as low as <$1100. Even a “thin and light” gaming laptop like the Legion 7 Slim w/ the R7 5800H and the 3060 goes on sale for $1400. You do get a very sleek design, but in terms of reliability, well the trackpad isn’t.
